utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I wish to address the court before we get on with evidence. At the very end of trial yesterday, the last page, 132, I think there is an error in the transcript. We didn't react in a timely manner. We must have been too tired to do so. I'm just waiting for the updated version of the last page, and the last of the transcript to be listened to. 132 of the draft transcript, line 18, the interpretation says, "The order was loud and clear, both for Vezmarevic and for Major Karanfilov." We in the courtroom heard this, "The order was loud and clear, issued by both Vukosavljevic and Karanfilov. That was what we heard and we believe this to be very important. I advised Mr. Moore of this, and I think he even agreed with me and confirmed that this was indeed what he heard too. That's one thing. And another thing, I'm speaking for all three teams. We received a letter from the OTP yesterday about their obligation to inform us of any future witnesses. This has been a relatively smooth exercise so far, and we would normally be given a schedule for the next 15 days. But the OTP informed us that they were in no position to tell us which witnesses would be coming over the next two weeks except for next Monday. After that we would probably be hearing witness Strinovic. They have lists of witnesses to come over the next weeks, but they can't say for certain. I'm sorry that Mr. Moore is not around. Mr. Weiner, whom I would like to wish a warm welcome could the courtroom is probably not in a position to provide these answers. What we really want to know as we've already pointed out, when OTP military experts are here to testify, we need at least a 15-day advance notice. We would like to have our experts present during those hearings and, as you know, we need to provide visas for them and there is a special procedure that we need to follow. It is for this reason that we would like the OTP to please give us advance notice of any experts coming here to testify. That's all I wish to say. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner, indeed, welcome. Are you in a position to deal, first, with the matter of the transcript? I would expect not.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No, I think I will have to look into both matters at the break, Your Honour, or sometime during the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, with the matter, the second matter, the arrival of expert witnesses, it will indeed be important that some better indication is possible than merely an identification -- here is the answer to your need. Mr. Moore, welcome. Two matters have been raised by Mr. Lukic. The first is an error in the transcript, which he believes you recognised when it was discussed late yesterday, the naming of a person who gave an order. Vezmarevic appears in the transcript; Vukosavljevic, it is said, was said in court. I don't know whether you are in a position to agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Dealing with the first point, I do agree with my learned friend that it was not Vezmarevic. From memory, it was Vukosavljevic and Karanfilov.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: That's certainly my recollection, but obviously it's subject to checking the accurate transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The second point is the forthcoming Prosecution witnesses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I know about that problem as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And a concern that there needs to be time to enable the Defence to get their experts here to hear the evidence of yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Now, they say at the moment you are not in the position to give an indication when yours are arriving. Can you assist us?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Clearly it depends on the length of time that what I will call lay witnesses will take. The two military experts that we will be calling will be Theunens, who is what I will call in-house and readily available, and Major General Pringle. Major General Pringle was, from memory, targeted for the 5th to the 9th of June, inclusive. He has got professional difficulties in relation to that. So -- and I wanted to finish the case with him, for various reasons. He would be able to do the week after that. So the way that the matters stand, we had hoped that we would be finished, as I said, within the first week of June, with our timetable. We have some outstanding witness difficulties. They should be resolved, I hope. Next week will be Strinovic and Grujic [Realtime transcript read in error, "Vujic"] after the video testimony on the Monday. That has -- that date has been broken, I think, three or four time, through no fault of OTP. So next week, should -- well, certainly Strinovic next week and that will take, I hope, for three days. May I just clarify one small matter? I've just had a message passed to me and I just would like to clarify one point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It will be Strinovic next week, Grujic has got certainly difficulties. It may well be that there can be element of accommodation in relation to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Sorry, the -- is it Grujic or Vujic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each appear in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: It's Grujic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: So it will be -- the witness giving video evidence next Monday, Monday, part of Tuesday, it should then be Mr. Strinovic -- Mr. Smith is dealing with this area. That will be Tuesday, and part of Wednesday morning, I would have thought. And the, I would hope conclusion of cross-examination by Thursday, Friday. I don't know the extent of the cross-examination on that. May I just set Grujic to the side for a moment, because one is trying to fit him in, because of his professional obligations. We had hoped for the two of them to come together. There is an application for two witnesses whose names escape me. They relate to the blue folder. That is the material that was sent to Zagreb from the Vukovar Hospital, as we submit, and that was to do with the creation of the documentation. My learned friends wanted, and indeed I think the Court and all wanted to find out the source material on that. There are two witnesses on that. We don't know if my learned friends require those witnesses, or if they now accept the content of those statements as being accurate and justifying the document. So we don't know what the situation is on that. They've only received the statement, and I don't expect that they will have an answer immediately for that. Those two witnesses are a variable on time that I am not able to assist the Court on. If we were calling them in chief, I would like to think we could do it almost in a quasi-89 (F) format to target them on specific topics but there must be, I would have thought, three days' evidence there. But as I say, it may well be now that the Defence, having seen the documentation, will agree to the document going in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Next week then, if I understand you, there's the videolink for two and a bit days.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps not quite as much as that, but approximately two days.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Okay. And then?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Strinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Will continue and clearly finish the week.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I would have thought, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The week following that, the 22nd. Sorry, the week following that. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I had a heart attack, almost. The week following that there are civilian witnesses. There is Hartman, who has to give evidence, and there are two other witnesses to deal with other matters and I don't wish to go into the details of that. I can't honestly put hand on heart and say exactly who they are and what they deal with, but I certainly had discussions about it. That should see that week out. And then you go into the military witnesses and the difficulty with Pringle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Theunens, how long are you seeing there?

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: I will be dealing with Theunens, and that would be -- I want to deal with it in the following way, if there is no objection, that I will put in the report, the expert's report, I will use the e-court to deal with the documentation. I would have thought, in chief, I would hope I would finish Theunens within a day, but can I please not be held to that, because when it comes to documentation and military language it's not always easy to estimate. But Theunens is a fairly substantial witness and goes in, in significant detail. I would have thought myself that Theunens will be, if there is military experts for the Defence, I would have thought myself that you must be looking at three days' cross-examination. Perhaps two, three, something like that. And Pringle, again, I will deal with Pringle. Again, in chief I would anticipate that a day in chief will not be far away on the estimate. Again, cross-examination with experts advising, I'm not able to assist, but again, I would have thought it will be analogous in time to the Theunens situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: So we would either lose two to three days in the week of the 5th and the 9th, or there will be the two additional witnesses, should you be granted leave and should the Defence wish them called.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: There are other witnesses, but they're small witnesses, if I may use that phrase, where I'm trying to move them into spaces so that I don't lose any time. I am trying to keep the military witnesses to specific times so that we know exactly the timetable for the Defence experts. I would have thought myself that if one is looking the week commencing the 5th, if it is the week commencing the 5th, that will be when the military witnesses will commence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And Pringle, you're suggesting, the week following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes, I'm afraid so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Which may be commencing the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Each of us is without calendar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. So those are the time estimates.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: And that would be then the last witness of your case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: If there is one other -- there may be one other witness, but it is a very short witness, but it will be finishing very, very soon, within one or two days after Pringle. I'm not saying definitively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Both Defence counsel and the Chamber would appreciate greater clarity, as some of these imponderables become clearer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MOORE
utterances.text: Yes. No, it is our intention to do that. But we are waiting for phone calls, trying to get people in on timetables, and it's not always easy to get definite answers from people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Lukic, that has given you more to go on for your experts, if it is Monday the 5th or whichever the date is, of June. That week and the week following seems to be the dates for your experts. Now, Mr. Moore mentioned a motion which has arrived for two additional witnesses. Could we indicate that we would want the Defence response by next Monday on that. That's a shortened time to respond, but it's a relatively straightforward issue. Thank you very much for your assistance. Is it time for your debut, Mr. Weiner?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will get you a witness, with any luck.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: While the witness is on the way, Your Honour, this expert witness, Mark Wheeler, his testimony was accepted or admitted pursuant to your decision of 21 October 2005. This is a 92 bis of a 94 bis expert testimony. His expert report. So it will be a very short or brief examination-in-chief, since his testimony is in and his report is admissable, approximately 15 to 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Exhibit 391; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The report and CV, however, are not in, Your Honour. His report and CV have not been admitted. His prior testimony has.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you please read aloud the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Good morning, doctor, could you state your name for the record?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: My name is Mark Crawford Wheeler.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you tell us where you live?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I live in Sarajevo, Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And where do you work?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I work in the office of the High Representative as a political adviser although actually paid by the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And how long have you been living in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I've been living in Bosnia on this occasion since April 2001. I was there in the tail -- at the tail-end of the war as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us what years you lived in Bosnia prior to this period of 2001?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, during the war I lived in Croatia in the latter part of 1994, in Central Bosnia in late 1995, in Sarajevo in 1996 and early 1997, and then again in Croatia, Vukovar, in fact, in spring of 1997.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, or doctor, did you ever serve as an academic historian?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I worked as a historian of Southeastern Europe and Eastern Europe generally, modern history of that part of the world in the universities of Lancaster, London, and Derby between 1994 -- excuse me, 1975 and 1994, and then again, 1997, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, could you tell us what your highest degree is?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I hold a Ph.D. in history from the university of Cambridge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And what was the subject of your thesis?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It was on British foreign policy towards in Yugoslavia in the Second World War and particularly the British decision to abandon Draza Mihajlovic and support Josip Broz Tito and his Partisans.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, sir, have you ever published any books, papers, or articles on the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, quite a few and they are in my CV, I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown ERN number 0600-1130-0600-1136? Which is also tab number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There is an alert on the transcript, doctor, that your speech tends to be a little fast.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I see that now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My students always complained of that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: If you could just slow it down to the pace of my mind, that would be very good. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't think I can comment on that without risking insult.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Doctor, do you recognise the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I certainly do.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Could the registrar just move through the pages? Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Doctor, what is that document?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is my curriculum vitae.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And who prepared that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And is that the most recent version?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It is the most recent version that I sent to this court, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We would like to offer that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honour, this CV will become Exhibit Number 446.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, have you testified previous live before the ICTY?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I testified in the case against Slavko Dokmanovic as an expert witness in January, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And did you prepare a report for that testimony?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I did, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And when was that prepared?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I wrote it at the end of December 1997, early January 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Can the witness be shown tab 2, which is English 0210-9652- 0210-9682, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Doctor, are you able to recognise the document on the screen?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I can, indeed, yes. It is the report I prepared.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, it's approximately eight years since you prepared the report. Do you still stand by the opinions and informations contained in that report?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: By and large, yes. I don't see any reason to have too many second thoughts about the contents of the report. Certainly I would stand by the major argument. We can -- of course, now with the benefit of both hindsight and the huge amount of research that has been done on the wars in the former Yugoslavia, there are many things that could be amended, updated, more nuanced approaches introduced, but by and large I think the report stands the test of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, Doctor, there are no footnotes in that report. Could you tell us what the source of the information was that you used to develop that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, much of the historical background simply reflects the fact that I had been active in researching and teaching the history of the former Yugoslavia since the early 1970s. The specifics regarding the coming of the war of the 1990s and the specifics regarding events in Eastern Slavonia came from journalistic accounts that had been published at time. The secondary literature that was already available that incorporated an awful lot of memoir literature, and in some cases that had been provided to me by the Prosecution to help me prepare that report. But the bulk of it of course, relates to historical background which was well-known to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: The Prosecution would like to offer that document at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 447 Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Doctor, would I like to discuss with you just one issue, and then we'll turn you over to the Defence for cross-examination. Just spend a few minutes on one issue. In your report, and in your previous testimony which has been admitted, there is discussion concerning military activity which occurred in Eastern Slavonia. We'll start off with Eastern Slavonia, between August 1st, actually from mid-July 1991 through November 21st, 1991. Could you tell us about that, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, I tried in my report to put the coming of the war to Eastern Slavonia in the context of how it had spread in Croatia generally. Particularly of course after the short, sharp war in Slovenia. So the major -- the major fighting in Eastern Slavonia comes after the 27th of June, 1991. Although it has to be said there were provocation and incidents and even some killings going on in the region of Eastern Slavonia from May, 1991. But the real escalation of the war starts after the end of the war in Slovenia, so we're talking about from July 1991. And at that point of course we get major engagement by the Yugoslav People's Army, the JNA, not just as had been in the early stages in much of Croatia where it sought to interpose itself between alarmed and rebelling Serbs and the authorities, the police authorities of the new Tudjman government. But it also started now taking an active hand in conquering territory from July.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And could you just tell us about the engagement in certain villages of the military actions in certain villages between that time period, mid-July through November 21st?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, as I already indicate you had, the JNA was seeking to occupy territory, and that meant of course investing and taking villages. It was doing so of course in alliance with the remnants of the old Territorial Defence structure that had gone over to the Serb side, as well as various paramilitary formations, both locally generated, but the most notorious of which of course were sent in from Serbia itself, with a connivance of one or another political party or security structure or the Serbian Interior Ministry of the MUP to do this kind of activity. And what was notable about what last happening in Eastern Slavonia was the intermingling, the commingling, the joint effort on the part of both these paramilitary forces on the one hand and the JNA on the other.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned Eastern Slavonia. It's neighbour, Western Slavonia, was there any military activity occurring during that same time period; mid-July through November 21st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. The -- it was in August I believe of 1991 that the local Serb rebels, the militia, I guess it would be fair to call them, helped by the Banja Luka Corps of the JNA, seized the crucial communications centre of Okucani in Western Slavonia which had the effect of breaking the road, motorway, and rail -- main-line rail links between the capital, Zagreb, and Eastern Slavonia. And as a consequence the -- the stage appeared to be being set for a larger Serb-led conquest of Croatia. But the interesting thing that happened in, in Eastern Slavonia -- excuse me, in Western Slavonia, is that by the end of November the territory that the Serbs had been carving out for themselves was significantly reduced. In fact the territory all the way from the border with Bosnia-Herzegovina up to Veravidica [phoen] was halved in size as the Serbs withdrew under some Croatian pressure from the area between Veraidica down to Daruvar and then to Pakrac. And Pakrac became effectively the northern limit of Serb-controlled territory in Western Slavonia. And this is historically significant, I think, in retrospect, because it marked the end of wider Serb ambitions for carving out even more territory in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And we've talked about two areas in Croatia. Was there any other military activity in Croatia, outside of western and Eastern Slavonia during that period, mid-July, 1991 through November 21st, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, of course there was. And the most notorious as far as the international public was concerned was the artillery offensive, naval offensive directed against Dubrovnik in the southern Adriatic, and that of course occupied the world's television screens at that time. Foreigners, of course, all knew about Dubrovnik. Many hundreds and hundreds of thousands of them thousands, perhaps millions had been tourists there. So this brought the war home to people abroad in a way that hadn't been the case during the previous couple of months of the siege of Vukovar, for example. Dubrovnik became an international scandal and there was much breast-beating. The military significance of the shelling of Dubrovnik was really pretty marginal. One would have thought it was much more politically significant. It was meant to do two things. It was meant to punish the Zagreb regime, but it was also meant to implicate the Montenegrins who had previously held aloof from the war in the struggle by giving them something to do. But at the same time, of courses, the campaign was going on from the bases of Serb control in Northern Dalmatia, Dalmatinska Zagora, through Lika, and Kordun into Baranja. So more territory was also being taken at that time, across the southern flank of Croatia, you know, the-- south of Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: May the witness be shown Exhibit 312, please?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: If I might correct myself, I said "Baranja." I meant Banja, through Lika and Kordun into Banja. Baranja had, of course, itself been an area which the JNA had seized in August, I think it was, 1991. Baranja being the Croatian part of Baranja, since the district is split with Hungary.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: We have copies of the exhibit for the judges and counsel, if they would like.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Doctor, did you have any knowledge as to the information contained in this exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Not specifically. It's not a document that I saw before yesterday. But it strikes me as an accurate summary of the way in which the JNA and the paramilitaries worked together in order to intimidate villagers, make as many as possible flee, to then occupy the territory, and generally carry out what would later become known as ethnic cleansing.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: And finally, Doctor, is this consistent with your opinion and your report that you filed?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, it is. If I might just add. The exact scenario might vary occasionally from place to place, but this is an accurate summary in which the way in which region by region, village by village, town by town conquests took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Weiner. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Good morning, professor. My name is Vladimir Domazet, I am one of the counsel appearing for Mr. Mrksic, and on behalf of Mr. Mrksic's defence I will put some questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the defence teams have attempted to expedite and facilitate these proceedings by dividing among themselves the topics for cross-examination. I hope that the Defence teams will not overlap in their questions or that they will do so very little. I will put questions about one segment of what Mr. Wheeler presented in his oral testimony and his written report dated January 1998, and used in the Dokmanovic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Professor, from your CV and your previous experience and current work, it's evident that your experience is truly impressive, as is your persistence, because, as I see, you have mastered the language, which is not easy, but which is certainly of assistance to you and has been in your work to date. I assume that you are able to use your knowledge of the language to contact and interview not only your colleagues and statesmen, but, so to say, the common people, the local population throughout this period, and that this is one of your sources of knowledge on the basis of which you wrote your report. Am I right in thinking this?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: In part, yes, Mr. Domazet. The mere fact that I lived in Vukovar for admittedly a short period in the spring of 1997 and was able to talk to quite a lot of people, including, it has to be said, one of my colleagues at the time, Drago Hedl who has subsequently of course revealed receive through Feral tribune and international publications about what happened in Eastern Slavonia in 1991 and 1992. I did learn quite a bit from both -- with people whom I lived in Vukovar, for example, as well as some of my UN colleagues at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor. This certainly refers to the period you spent in Vukovar. It seems, however, that you spent most of your time on the territory of the countries of the former Yugoslavia in Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather the Federation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, given the fact that I've now lived consistently in Sarajevo since 2001, in chronological terms you're right. But my earlier academic existence, I was -- actually spent much more time in Belgrade where I was a post-graduate student back in 1972 and 1973. During the latter stages of the war I was actually -- the latter stage of the war of 1990s, I was actually based in -- in Western Slavonia, Nova Gradiska, so I actually saw the fall of Western Slavonia on the 1st of May, 1995, during operation Blesak. So I have some experience other than just in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, certainly this is what I wanted to ask, because this is not evident from your CV, that you spent time in Serbia. My question is, how much time did you spend in Serbia and how useful was this in your research and in your reaching the conclusions that you did in your reports?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, it was in Serbia where I lived in the summer of 1970 and then again during 1972 and 1973 when I was doing research for my doctoral thesis that I actually learned the language, the language that we used to call Srpsko-Hrvatski. For the purposes, however, of the report I prepared in the case of Slavko Dokmanovic, other than the fact that living there, living in the former Yugoslavia previously helps one understand the basic set of circumstances, this residence in Serbia long before had not any particular relevance to my report in the Dokmanovic case. In fact, during a large part of the war I was persona non grata and unable to get a visa to go to the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, although I did actually visit Belgrade for a couple of weeks in the summer of 1997, when I could get a visa.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I understand you correctly, Professor, your visit to Serbia was almost 20 years before the relevant events. At the relevant time, unfortunately for the reasons you have adduced, you did not have an opportunity to see that side at close range. You mentioned that you were persona non-grata at the time. Was this an official evaluation, and can you tell us at least in your opinion why this happened? I think it might be important for us to find out.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that anyone knows very often whether such a status is official or not. I was simply told on many occasions in 1992, 1993, by the then Yugoslav embassy in London that I would not receive a visa. But when you say, of course, that I -- my actual long period of residence in Serbia was, you know, long before the events of the early 1990s, you are, of course, correct. But as an academic interested in the history of Southeastern Europe and Yugoslavia in particular, I suspect not a single year went by between the early 1970s and the early 1990s that I was not at least once in that year in Belgrade, or someplace else in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now I will go into your report as it relates to the beginning of 1998. And I will deal more with the historical part, the constitution will be dealt with by my colleague. So I will ask you first of all about some statistical data you dealt with, which is available to everyone. If I'm correct, according to you, in 1991 when you speak of the ethnic breakdown about 60.000 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: 600.000, interpreter's correction --

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- Serbs lived in Croatian. But in your view most of these did not live in the rural areas, and you go on to list areas of Northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, Banja, which, if you agree, are geographically contiguous, and you mention east and west Slavonia, Baranja and western Srem, which are at the far east end of Croatia and are also contiguous areas. Have I interpreted your report correctly in this area?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, you have indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: When you deal with northern Dalmatia, Lika, Kordun, and Banja, you did not include these rural areas by chance, I mean you did not say that they were rural areas by chance. These were predominantly rural areas inhabited by Serbs, in some cases a majority of Serbs. I think we can agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, and I called them rural areas because of course they are very sparsely populated and they are indeed rural, mountainous, extremely beautiful parts of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. And as regards the territory, it was not insignificant territory, it was a considerable amount of territory, but sparsely populated; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Although you say, and this is quite correct, that it was a smaller number of the population who inhabited those areas, and they really are beautiful areas, all the same we used to refer to these as passive areas, meaning poor areas. Is this, in your view, one of the reasons why people, especially younger people, left to go to larger towns all over Yugoslavia and also Croatia, which is why many Serbs lived in the larger towns in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Of course it is. The people from the so-called passive areas or the so-called dinaric regions after the Second World War when industrialisation and urbanisation took place on a large scale, were notable for their movements into the cities or into richer agricultural areas, for example Eastern Slavonia or Vojvodina. So-called colonists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. It is probably for this reason that the information you give, i.e., that over 50.000 Serbs lived in Zagreb at the time, and I'm referring to the census of 1991, while at the same time in the territories you call the rebel republic of Srpska Krajina, there were about 200.000. This is not a lot in territorial terms, but it is a significant number of Serbs in that area, would you agree? And did you get this figure by looking at the territory or in some other way?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, given the lapse of time, I don't actually now remember where I got that figure. What I do remember, however, because I then worked for a non-governmental organisation, which had many projects for which I was responsible in Western Slavonia, in Daruvar, Pakrac, Okucani, that I formed the very definite opinion that there were far fewer people living, at that point, this is in 1994, 1995, in Republika Srpska Krajina than the authorities of that rebel republic actually alleged. One of the effects of the wartime privations, one of the kind of would-be state that Republika Srpska Krajina was, was to encourage a continuing outflow of the populous, and so my own suspicion is that the population of Republika Srpska Krajina, apart from Eastern Slavonia, was very much less than we thought at the time. And the estimate of 200.000, I'm not terribly sure, as I said, where I got that. But that may even be an exaggeration. During the war, Republika Srpska Krajina was haemorrhaging people, most of whom were heading for Serb-controlled parts of Bosnia or, more especially, for Serbia itself. On the other hand, of course, a good many Serbs remained in big cities in Croatia; Zagreb, Pula, Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Based on what you indicate, and I'm referring to the status it cans, and of course we're talking about 1991. It appears that about one-third of all the Serbs lived outside the borders of the Republic of Serbia. Would that seem to be an accurate assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In your report, you say that this is an oft-stated fact to explain why they, the Serbs, I presume, more than all the others were never willing to give up Yugoslavia. Do you remember that particular explanation? Can you please comment on that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. You're right. The standard supposition, both among foreigners who studied Southeastern Europe and of course among many Yugoslavs themselves, was that the Serbs needed Yugoslavia vastly more than any other of the south Slav peoples. They needed it because only by having a Yugoslavia, could all Serbs live in the same state. And the supposition, therefore, was that any regime in Belgrade would work very hard to maintain Yugoslavia. The point of my argument in the report, of course, is that when Milosevic comes along, that old historical wisdom is no longer valid.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I would leave Milosevic aside, at least for the time being. In your report you talk about what could have been problems, potential problems, or what could have drawn this community closer together, or what could have led it to a crisis instead. You spoke about language, you spoke about religion. As far as language was concerned, I think I entirely agree with what you state in your report. Your assessment of what went on in those years particularly, and bearing in mind your explanation today that in the 1970s you spent a great deal of time in Yugoslavia, particularly in Serbia. I am sure you do remember the language problems that occurred at the time. It was raised at first as a scientific issue and constituted a new battle-ground, as it were, between linguists in Croatia on the one hand and Serbia on the other. Would I be right in saying that, sir? Do you agree that this language issue, although you don't necessarily view that as anything crucial, was no major issue? If we forget about Slovenia and Macedonia for a moment, that was not a major problem because the languages were similar and could be used in communication smoothly, but do you agree that this constituted a point of departure for this sort of crisis, especially in the 1970s and onwards?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. You're correct. Fighting over language, or I should say arguing over language was one of the ways in which the re-emergeance of the national question in socialist Yugoslavia was given, quite literally, expression. The breakdown of the so-called Novi Sad agreement of 1954, for example, which the Croats renounced, I think it was, at beginning of 1970s, as you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Professor. Furthermore, it is a fact that two different scripts were used, the Latin script and the Cyrillic script, which only proved to be an additional source of trouble in purely ethnic terms, since one or the other was predominantly used by the different groups. Would you agree with me that the two different scripts, although they were defined as equal in some of the republican constitutions, particularly the Croatian constitutions, were not quite equal after all and that this may have proved to be an additional source of inter-ethnic strife or conflict. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I would. Particularly because, as far as Serbs were concerned, not just in Croatia, or just in Bosnia-Herzegovina, but also in Serbia itself, there was concern that the Latin alphabet was achieving primacy over the Cyrillic in too many popular publications, and scientific publications as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: The Latin alphabet was officially used in the JNA throughout its existence; do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. As for religion, which is another topic that you tackled, I think your assessments are quite fair. You may, although, have omitted to consider this: A significant portion of the population at the time were atheists, people who wanted nothing to do with religion, for the most part, no doubt, on account of their commitment to communism, the official ideology at the time. You must be familiar with this phenomenon, right?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are correct to suggest that an awfully large portion of the population all over the former Yugoslavia were not practicing, whether it be practicing Roman Catholics, Muslims, or Orthodox. But they were all conscious in virtually every case of what their religious heritage was. I don't think it would therefore be fair to say that there was a large body of atheists, there were a large bodies of people who were entirely secular, but they knew what their religious origins were and saw the connection between their religious heritage and national identity, even if they were not practicing. And people who were not practicing formally nonetheless would take part in the principal festivals, you know non-practicing Muslims always celebrated Bajram. Non-practicing Serbs celebrated their family slava, non-practicing Catholics, Croats, certainly celebrated Christmas. But, of course, everybody celebrated Christmas.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I tend to agree with you. I particularly agree that some areas to a larger extent, perhaps, than some others areas to a lesser extent did celebrate religious holidays, but you probably know that some were trying to keep their religious convictions well concealed, or celebrated in secrecy, since religious holidays at the time did not coincide with state or official bank holidays, if you like.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're right. There -- but of course this need to dissemble about one's religious belief lessened over time. It was no longer a big problem after the early 1960s, certainly. And in any case the problem only arose only for card-carrying members of the League of Communists. They were the ones who might have felt it necessary to pretend that they were not religious believers. Ordinary people had no such problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps, Mr. Wheeler, perhaps. But there were a lot of those extraordinary people, if I may call them that, who weren't ordinary people, those people were afraid, they didn't dare go to church or anything because of the official positions that they held at the time. I would like to wrap this up though, there's something else you say in your report, something that you obviously studied. Do you believe this to be typical? Do you perhaps believe this to be unique? What am I talking? At the time when you spent time in Yugoslavia, the Muslims, and this was a religious descriptor at the time, at one point became a nation, if you like. An individual nation and the descriptor used was still the same. I suppose you would agree with me that this was not entirely usual or habitual to combine national identity with religious identity to quite this extent. Would that strike a chord with you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're correct, Mr. Domazet that this was a strange phenomenon as using a religious designation as a -- simultaneously as a national designation. And it's one of the reasons why I think Muslims by 1993 decided that they must revive the term Bosnjak from Habsburg times to describe themselves, so that they had a national designation which was not exclusively religious.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That is perfectly accurate, Professor. But a lot of time went by before this term, the term Bosniak, really started being used, and it began to be used in Serbia around Novi Pazar and this had nothing do with Bosnia itself because some people actually believed the term Bosniak to be related to Bosnia, exclusively, which of course is erroneous. Thank you, Professor, I would now like to move on to the historical framework or context which I believe to have a great bearing on the events in the former Yugoslavia. I will first try to deal with what you called yourself have called the first Yugoslavia, the state that was established after World War II.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction, after World War I.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I would like to go through some facts -- I said World War I, there may have been an error in the interpretation. Is it true that Serbia or the Kingdom of Serbia at the time in World War I sided with the allies, Great Britain, France and all the other countries fighting against Germany and the Austro-Hungarian Empire.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, the Kingdom of Serbia was the original allied power.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Of course we should not forget Montenegro. I do not want to lead to other rifts, especially not between our own Defence teams, since some us are actually Montenegrins. They also sided with the allied powers, and I suppose we can agree that the cause that led to the outbreak of war was the assassination in Sarajevo, right?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, the assassination in Sarajevo in 20th of June 1914 provided the occasion for the war indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And this was the reason that the war broke out in purely practical terms in Serbian territory, the Austro-Hungarian army attacked Serbia sometime in the summer of 1914. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I hope we agree that at the time the present territory of Slovenia, Croatia and even Bosnia and Herzegovina to a large extent belonged to the Austro-Hungarian Empire. I am sure you are aware of the fact that soldiers mobilised from those areas were always members of the Austro-Hungarian army at the time, Slovenes, Croats, perhaps I should not use the term Bosniaks, but anyway people who lived in the area. Would that be a fair assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, that's a perfectly fair assessment. And it's why, of course, the First World War was also, as far as the south Slav peoples were concerned, a form of civil war. Because, given the large volunteer regiments of Croats and Slovenes that joined the Serbian forces after the period on Corfu and fought on the Salonika front, you therefore had Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes fighting for a Serbia, a future south Slav state, as well as Serbs, Croats, Slovenes, and Bosnjaks fighting in the ranks of the Habsburg armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: By all means, sir. I'm not trying to say that those who fought with the allied powers most of them at least wanted to achieve that, but they were citizens of that state, they were military conscripts. It was their duty to sign up. A lot of those people surrendered or changed sides and sided after a while with the Serbian army; I'm sure you are aware of that group as well. What you have referred to, the volunteers, yes, that may well be an historical fact, but this also includes families who lived on other continents outside of Slovenia or Croatia. There were people who lived in other continents who arrived at this point in time in Europe to join the army. Would I be correct in stating that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Professor. Are you familiar with the fact that much later, the great Yugoslav leader Josip Broz Tito also fought as a non-commissioned officer with the Austro-Hungarian army along the Serb front. He was later moved to the Russian front where he was eventually wounded and captured. Are you familiar with this information, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Finally, this war that broke out midway through 1914, is it true that this small state of Serbia, together with Montenegro, put up resistance almost up until the end of 1915, when it was forced to withdraw to leave these areas and across Albania to withdraw to Corfu and Greece since Bulgaria had by this time entered the war from the right flank which had, up to this point in time, been neutral, which further aggravated Serbia's position. Is that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You will probably agree that, following this, Greece and Corfu were places that not only the soldiers, but also the leaders in exile started to gather and the same thing applied to many Croats and Slovenes who shared this Slavic idea of unification. Even before the war was over and negotiations had started to promote this idea. Would that seem to be a correct assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed the case, yes. And, in fact, the defeat of Serbia and the exile of the Serbian government to Corfu facilitated this process of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes from the Habsburg monarchy, the so-called south Slav committee, getting together with the Pasic government in Serbia at the time and coming up with, ultimately in 1917, the Corfu declaration looking for the creation of a common south Slav state.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Certainly, Professor. You're talking about the Corfu declaration, no doubt, that is how we refer to it, which provided foundation for the so-called first Yugoslavia. You are an historian who dealt with all these things, and this is something that in Serbia, of all places, perhaps you had occasion to hear during your time there. I am talking about the misgivings about many of the Croatian and Slovene leaders who advocated that sort of state. They may have done this for purely tactical reasons, since up to this point in time they had never had a state of their own. They were, in fact, on the losing side in that war because they had sided with the Austro-Hungarian Empire and refused to side with Serbia and Montenegro in order it create a state. This also applies to the territorial aspect of the situation. We have Italy, who decided at one point to side with the allies and asked for Dalmatia in return. Perhaps you could comment on that, sir.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, before the First World War, there were many more Croats who were vastly more interested or very interested in creating a common south Slav state than there were Serbs, and as the war proceeded it became an urgent necessity for both Croats and Slovenes because the integrity of their national territory was threatened by the secret treaty of London and the promises that had been made to the Italians, and so they indeed needed very quickly to get in bed with Serbia, to get -- to be able to switch from the losing side of the war to the winning side of the war, as you indicated. But, of course, as you have also -- as we've -- as we have already mentioned this morning, there were large numbers of Serbs in these Habsburg territories that were desperately looking for a national solution for themselves, given the fact that in October of 1918 the Habsburg monarchy fell apart. There was revolutionary threats in Hungary, virtually everybody's territory west of the river Drina was under tremendous threat under some rapacious neighbour. So Yugoslavia, the creation of the Yugoslav state became an urgent necessity for those people who had formerly lived under the Habsburg monarchy, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly slow down for the benefit of the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will try.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We have some minutes to go before the break. I will try to finish this set of questions. But most of all I would like to thank you for your comment and your elucidations, Professor. Can we agree that even at the time there were those in Serbia who advocated the creation of a Serbian state. At the time, since Serbia was on the winning side, this state would have included areas with Serbian population from the former Austro-Hungarian Empire which would have roughly corresponded with the borders what is now termed Greater Serbia. Greater or smaller, at any rate, it certainly would have been greater than it ended up in 1918, would it not?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes indeed. There is no doubt there were very many people in the Serbian government, including Nikola Pasic himself, who were interested in incorporating largely Serb-inhabited territories in southern Hungary, in Eastern Slavonia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and, of course, in Montenegro as well, than they were interested in the idea that Croatian intellectuals had propagated since the 1830s about a common south Slav home.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Do you believe that in view of the circumstances that prevailed at the time it would have been possible not to create this greater state of Serbs, Slovenes, and Croats but a somewhat smaller state that would have nonetheless been bigger in terms of size than the previous Kingdom, the Serbian Kingdom, including Eastern Slavonia, the parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and probably some other areas too?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It would have been possible, but it would have flown in the face of the trends, of course, taking place at the end of the war. Because after all, the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes is formed after a series of genuine acts of self-determination on the part of the peoples of the Habsburg monarchy. Their conventions held in Ljubljana, Zagreb, Sarajevo where people voted, actually, to join with Serbia. It would have been very strange for Serbia to have said no. And, of course, Prince Aleksandar, later King Aleksandar, did indeed say yes. It was of a piece, of course, of what was going on throughout the former Habsburg monarchy. This was -- after all, think of the way in which the Czechoslovak state has been formed at the same time, or for that matter the very large republic of Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I agree entirely with you, sir. I agree there was a majority in Serbia advocating this idea of a union. The same probably applied to Croatia and the Corfu declaration was eventually implemented.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just finished one set of my questions, and Your Honours, I believe this is a convenient time for us to take our first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will resume at 20 past.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Wheeler, we'll take this up where we left off. When answering my last question as to whether, regardless of the general tendency and desire on the part of the Serbs, and most Serb statesmen, to create a common state encompassing the Croats, Slovenes, and other south Slavs in this territory, we agreed that Serbia as the country on the winning side of this war, could have resolved this issue in a different way by including those Serbs who had lived beyond its borders up to that point, but, in fact, what they did was to create a common state. However, as you yourself observed, from the very beginning of the functioning of the state then called the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, problems began to arise, there was obstruction, and in particular this was done by Croatian representatives. In your report I think you adduced us some of the reasons; centralism, the dynasty, and the capital. My question is the following: You probably meant that the Karadjordjevic dynasty, the Serb dynasty was at the head of the state, the capital was in Belgrade, but my question is: Wasn't that something that had been agreed on, on Corfu, and later on, and that this was never actually an issue that was not agreed upon until the point of unification?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, you are again correct. The trouble was that once there were democratic elections in the new Yugoslav Kingdom in 1920 the people who had agreed the basis of unification were no longer the people who had the confidence of the masses. And we saw the rise of the Croatian Peasant Party in particular, which wanted effectively a renegotiation of the terms on which the peoples of the new Yugoslav state were coming together. There was also, of course, a radicalisation in the new country generally when lots of people voted for the communists. So the pact made in the extraordinary circumstances of war was something that a good many people in the new Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes waned to renegotiate, revisit. And certainly Stjepan Radic, the founder and leader of the Croatian Peasant Party, or Croatian People's Republican Peasant Party, as it styled itself occasionally at the time, certainly took the position that the basis for the unification should be reconsidered and they certainly also dissented from the so-called Vidovdan 1921 constitution which provided for a highly centralised state. This was a problem for Croats in particular, because they did not feel that they would be protected in the same way that Slovenes would, for example, by having a separate language. They would be much more under the thumb of a centralising minded government in Belgrade than Slovenia would, for example. It has to be said also that the Serbs of Croatia and of Bosnia-Herzegovina very much wanted a highly-centralised state. They thought that would be something that would protect them. They also tended to be in the form of people like Svetozar Pribicevic, ardent believers ion the idea of almost forcefully making Yugoslavs out of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. Of course at the time nobody considered Montenegrin or Macedonians or, for that matter, Bosnian Muslims to be anything than either Serbs or Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wheeler, in your report you put forward the idea that this was an attempt to find a viable political formula which would make it possible to express, recognise, adapt, and accept the situation that several closely-connected south Slav nations inhabited the same or adjacent territories. Do you recall that sentence from your statement? And, as you said, many of the proponents and protagonists of Yugoslav union in 1918 believed they were forging a nation as well as a state, and that a common Yugoslav identity would, with careful nurturing, emerge to subsume the separate, tribal, as you say, identities. Do you have any comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: No, I think that I certainly recall what I wrote, and I continue to agree with what I wrote then. If you want me to expand on it, I could simply say that this was a very common notion at time in east central Europe. Tomas Masaryk, the founder president of Czechoslovakia believed too that he was creating a new Czechoslovakia nation. The winners in the First World War all believed, if we're talking about Romania, Poland, Czechoslovakia, they were in the position to -- on what they saw as the west European model of the 19th century, to create a common nation. After all, France was the example they usually had in mind, whereby France, at the beginning of 19th century was itself a highly multi-national state with people speaking a variety of different languages but France had become a highly centralised state, a progressive state, and people in east central Europe wished to imitate the French example and make national and state boundaries coincide. For those countries which inherited very large national minorities, this was always going to be a very big problem, but in the case of countries like Yugoslavia and Czechoslovakia, the close affinity of the individual nations meant that it didn't really seem impossible in the circumstances of 1918, that the 19th century West European experience could be replicated and a state could also become a single nation.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. From your CV I see that you are a citizen of the U.S., and you yourself know what happened in the U.S., where there were many nations but a single national identity emerged. Unfortunately in this case it did not happen. My question is as follows: This idea of a Yugoslav identity, would you agree with me that it was not an idea that aimed at creating Serbs out of all the other Slavs, but an effort to create a new Yugoslav nation out of all -- all the nations there, including the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Certainly those Serbs, Croats and Slovenes who believed passionately in a Yugoslav state also tended in the early 20th century to believe passionately in creating a new Yugoslav national identity which would take the best from the pre-existing nations or tribes. The trouble was that far too many Serbs believed that a Yugoslav national identity should effectively be a Serb national identity and wished to Serbianise, if I can put it that way, their new fellow citizens in the new Yugoslav state, which of course then gave rise to the national question, which as far as most Serbs were concerned, was simply the Croat question in the inter-war years. Because the Croats, having invented the idea of a Yugoslav state, were the ones who believed that a Yugoslav state could only endure and prosper if it were a genuinely collective enterprise and not some form of Serbian domination.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I don't know if I understood you properly. At that time do you feel that the Croats were more in favour of this idea than the Serbs, whereas I think it was just the opposite. Perhaps it was a romantic idea at the time, this idea of creating Yugoslavs rather than an attempt to Serbianise all others.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are right. It certainly was a romantic idea, it was an idea of romantic intellectuals. But there was more of those romantic intellectuals amongst the Croats. The trouble, of course, as I indicated in the previous reply was that the -- the Yugoslav idea was something which many intellectuals amongst all of the south Slav peoples had in common. Unfortunately when democracy was let lose in 1920s with elections which saw vastly more people with the right to vote than had ever been the case before, the big political parties that emerged from this first free elections tended to have different ideas. In other words, the masses, whether we're talk about the mass of Croat peasants or the mass of Serbian peasants or the mass of Slovene peasants, hadn't been consulted. And that's when the trouble arose, when they started getting the vote and started wanting parties to advocate their interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I can agree with you there. It's well known how people can be manipulated, especially people desirous of prosperity who had just emerged from a very difficult war. However, let me ask you what you meant when, in your report, you said that you thought this did not happen because of numerous national dissatisfactions, as you say, which had existed in the Habsburg and Ottoman Empires. That is national discontents which troubled the Habsburg and Ottoman predecessors. Why do you mention the Ottoman predecessors in light of the fact that Serbia had long since liberated itself from its Ottoman rulers and had been independent quite a long time before the First World War? That's why I fail to understand why you mention Ottoman predecessors when referring to national discontents.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Oh, very simple because, of course, technically the Ottoman Empire up until 1908 had been the owner of Bosnia-Herzegovina, up until the Balkan Wars it had also held all of Macedonia and Kosovo, Kosovo-Metohija. So in other words the Ottoman inheritance was one that might have been fairly distance for narrow Serbia, but it was highly relevant in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Macedonia, and Kosovo. The Habsburg inheritance of course, was more recent. But what I was trying to explain in that passage was that Yugoslavia became a form of multi-national empire, just as the Ottoman Empire had been a vast multi-national empire, and the Habsburg monarchy had been a vast multi-national empire. It's simply that states like the Kingdom of the Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes, and the vastly expanded Romania, and the new Czechoslovak state, they all inherited the fundamental multi-national problems or problems of having a multi-national population that their predecessors had had. They were only slightly smaller multi-national Empires than the Habsburgs or the Ottomans had ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. And when the Kingdom was created, I mentioned before the break, and I hope you will agree, that there were huge problems with establishing the borders of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, especially the western border, primarily with respect to Dalmatia, which was claimed by Italy, you mentioned the secret treaty, also parts of Koruska [phoen] and Slovene territory around lakes Bled and Bohinj, which ultimately was included in the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes. Would you agree?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes. And as we've already discussed, the chaotic wartime situation in 1918 meant that the new Kingdom proclaimed on the 1st of December, didn't indeed have formal borders. There was still a communist revolution going on in Hungary, so there could be no borders established with Hungary until 1921. It took plebiscites in southern Corinthia and southern Stiria [phoen] to establish the borders with the new Republic of Austria, plebiscites which were managed by the new League of Nations, and of course, the western frontiers with Italy around Trieste and Istria, the loss of Istria, in fact, Italy, and Dalmatia, these were not settled until the treaty of Rapallo in 1924. So the state had these border problems which was one of the principal reasons why Slovenes and Croats in particular were in the circumstances of 1918, as I said before, desperate to cling to the victorious Serbian Kingdom and to get the victorious Serbian army into the territories as quickly as possible to save them from either the Hungarian Bolshevik revolution or from the Italian imperialists.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for these explanations. I fully agree. Now, I would like your opinion as to whether had the Kingdom of Croats, Slovenes and Serbs not been established, would Dalmatia have become Italian territory rather than Croatian territory, if you research this issue, but I believe you have because the issue of Dalmatia was a very important one after World War I.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It's highly unlikely that Italy would have acquired very much of Dalmatia, largely because the so-called big three, that is Lloyd George, Woodrow Wilson, and Clemenceau -- Georges Clemenceau were determined not to give Italy as much as it was demanding. So, in fact, the new Yugoslav state had some friends at the Paris peace conference. The fact that the Italians ended up getting as much as they did, in other words a saliert [phoen] around Zadar and kept all of Istria was a result that Woodrow Wilson felt compelled to give some concessions to the Italians, but there was no readiness not to give the Italians everything they demanded.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But my question was, had the Yugoslav state not been created, and it was formed by Serbia as the victorious country which asked for Croatia and Slovenia, parts of Slovenia, had not this been done, would not Italy have found it much easier to achieve its goals and get Dalmatia, and I believe that they did manage that in 1941.?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are completely correct, Mr. Domazet, had there been no Yugoslav state, had the Slovenes and Croats not allied themselves with the Serbian army and of course, had not the Habsburg monarchy fell away and fall apart in the chaotic way it did, then the Italians would indeed have scored much larger gains.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wheeler. We will now move on to another topic. You discussed the first Yugoslavia, which actually received its name a little later, but when speaking about centralism, I wish to ask you about decentralization. How was that state decentralized. I'm referring to the banovinas.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: The banovinas were created as a result of King Aleksandar's proclamation of a dictatorship in January of 1929, the Sestojanuarska Diktatura. He then went on to rearrange, during the year of 1929, the territorial structure of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, creating a series of provinces or banovina, which were meant to be shorn or have their historical national -- historical national territorial arrangements got rid of. The banovina were intended in other words to make people forget that they lived in a historic region called Slavonia or Central Croatia or Dalmatia or Montenegro or Bosnia-Herzegovina. The banovina were arranged in the interests of administrative efficiency, but also in the interests of getting rid of the loyalties that people might have had to particular historical territories. And finally at the end of 1929 Aleksandar moved -- King Aleksandar took the final step and changed the name of the country to the Kingdom of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Was it precisely for this reason that the names of the banovinas were for the most part, if I'm correct, the names of rivers. The Sava, Danube, Moravska, Vrbaska banovina, and so on? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed the case, yes, as well as in the case of -- there was a Primorska as well. And the idea was to create provinces which would be efficient for administration, which would, as I said, get rid of the notion that these Yugoslav tribes were still terribly important, and would make it easier for a highly centralised regime to govern the country.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe this was the beginning of regionalism, which is still topical in present-day Europe, but apparently it was an unsuccessful attempt, because according to you, the banovinas were a failure, or am I wrong? Would you please comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: The banovinas were certainly a failure. And they were -- they were transparently designed in the way in which the borders were drawn, to create as many banovina as possible in which Serbs would form the majority, and as few as possible in which Croats in particular or Bosnian Muslims would form the majority. And that's why I refer to them as being an attempt to make centralism more efficient, rather than any real sort of regionalisation. The original territorial structure of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes had indeed recognised these traditional historical units in terms of the way in which the country was set up, where the introduction of the banovina in 1929 was meant to get rid of the salience or the importance of these old historical territorial units.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that for example the Drina banovina encompassed inhabitants from both banks of the river Drina, from present day Serbia and present day Bosnia and Herzegovina to a more or less equal extent?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. And of course very many banovina also incorporated -- many banovina which had Croatian majorities also incorporated large parts of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or for that matter large parts of Srem or Srijem. But the general effect of the borders of the banovina was to create more territorial units in which Serbs would be the majority.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, as you believe this, my question is, what kind of real authority did the banovinas have, how important was it who would be living on a certain territory and who important was it for the authorities in that area, did the banovinas have any legislative powers, can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You make a very valid point, Mr. Domazet. The banovinas were for administrative efficiency only, they were not possessed with any legislative powers. They had really very little significance until such time as, after King Aleksandar's assassination, there were negotiations on what became known as the Cvetkovic-Macek Sporazum, the Cvetkovic-Macek agreement which led to a merger of Croatian banovinas and created a very large Croatian-occupied area, which would have power devolved to it from the centre, it would have home rule. At that point the banovinas became crucially important because they were actually going to have some real authority that mattered to one of the principal nations living in Yugoslavia, in this case the Croats. Many Serbs, of course, at the time after the 1939 Sporazum wanted their own sort of banovina. Everybody wanted to have a banovina at that point, but of course the Second World War intervened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We'll come to this issue which is of great interest to me, your standpoint on the creation of the Croatian banovina, but as we're now talking about the organisation of the state, at the local level were there municipalities, Opstina and Srezeri [phoen] as a higher level territorial unit encompassing more than one municipality?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. The parliamentary crisis we mentioned, and the pressure of Croatian parties in particular led just before the outbreak of World War II to the creation of a large banovina, much larger than previously, which was even named the Croatian banovina, unlike the previous banovina names which were named after rivers or the sea. Now a Croatian banovina was established with borders going all the way up to Belgrade itself, if I'm not wrong. Could you explain under what circumstances this occurred, and how it affected relations at the time and later on?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: This was an -- the creation of the large Croatian banovina in 1939 was an attempt on the part of Prince Regent Paul Karadjordjevic to get rid of, to pacify, the greatest domestic Yugoslav problem of the day which was the Croat question. And he decided to make a separate piece with the largest Croatian party, the Croatian peasant party, in order to -- I don't want to put it -- maybe I will. I'll put it very cynically. He wanted to buy Croatian loyalty in view of the very, very stormy weather ahead, with Hitler obviously making demands all over the place. He wanted to put Yugoslavia on very much firmer foundations by ensuring the loyalty of the bulk of Croats to the Yugoslav state, as the Second World War drew near. What was also said at the time, of course, was that the Croatian banovina was only going to be the first of a series of such devolutions of powers to national historical units inside Yugoslavia, but of course it didn't happen, the war came first.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But can we agree that this was a considerable concession to Croatia, or to the Croatian parties, advocating the creation of the Croatian banovina under that very name, and including the territory that was created?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
