utterances.text: Indeed, it was a considerable concession. And one that Franjo Tudjman later on would talk about endlessly, whenever he wanted to talk about the territory in Bosnia-Herzegovina that he thought should belong to Croatia, or, for that matter, Srijem.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. That's what some of my questions are about. The creation of the Croatian banovina, did after all cause a lot of problems later on. Another question about this, since first and foremost we are focusing on Vukovar and the surrounding area. The banovina before the creation of the Croatian banovina, Vukovar and its surroundings, which banovina did that area belong to?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Oh, gosh. This is the kind of question that not any longer being a professional teaching historian makes it difficult for me. I think it was dravska [phoen], but I could be wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not dwell on that. I'll move on to a different topic, the beginning of World War II. In Yugoslavia the war broke out in 1941, later than in some other parts of Europe, in fact. I think you have spent a lot of time studying these subjects and you are perfectly familiar with the circumstances under which back in 1941 the government that you yourself described as the Cvetkovic-Marcek government made a pact on the 25th of March. In Yugoslavia's later history there were many different interpretations, some of them quite one-sided, I believe. Your assessment, as an historian, the Yugoslav government, the Cvetkovic-Marcek government and the Count Pavle who in some way replaced King Aleksandar as the head of state, were they pro-German, of a pro-German orientation? Were they indeed in favour of a pact like that, or did they have different views, but were simply left without a choice at the time? Left without a better alternative. What is your assessment of March 1941?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: My personal view is that Prince Paul and his government had no alternative but to sign the tripartite fact. They had negotiated strenuously to make that pact as inoffensive as possible. But they, of course, offended Serb national feeling in particular by doing so, and found themselves two days later, turned out of office when the March 27th coup d'etat took place and the young King Peter was proclaimed to be of change and a military-led government under Dusan Simic was set up. Of course, the immediate effect of the Martski Prevat [phoen] was, in fact, to cause Hitler to repent that he had given a good deal, of course no deal with Hitler was ever a deal you could believe would stay valid, but caused him in his fury immediately to invade and destroy Yugoslavia. Prince Paul and the Cvetkovic government had thought they could at least purchase some time but signing the tripartite pact. They knew in their heart of hearts they would be on the allied side, but those who disagreed with them, especially in the Yugoslav army and air force, were subjected to considerable British secret service pressure, they were impressed by the heroic resistance which the Greeks were putting up at the time and felt that they knew better. But my own view is that it might have indeed been better for all of the peoples of Yugoslavia had the war not come as immediately as it did to Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I believe I entirely agree with you on this. About this pact, can we agree that although I entirely agree, that it violated the Serbs' national pride, and this applied to others in what was then Yugoslavia, I suppose, since this was after all a pact made with a power that was hard to resist. But this did not constitute an act of occupation of the country as it was. This would have been something different. Troops would have been passing through, but the neutrality would have been preserved. Would I be right in claiming that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: No. And the reason is that one of the concessions which the then Yugoslav foreign minister Cinkar Markovic got from Ribbentrop was a pledge in the pact -- well, rather it was a secret side agreement to the pact by which the Germans and the Italians guaranteed that there would be no requests for troop transports through Yugoslavia. And the problem here was that the Yugoslav government was fearful that the Germans, the Italians, would use Yugoslav territory to launch a new offensive on Greece. Now, the trouble with this pledge not to demand troop transports was that nobody believed it, and certainly the people who carried out the coup d'etat didn't believe it. The British didn't believe, the Greeks didn't believe, and so therefore, although formally there was a pledge, there was some reason to believe it would be only a matter of time, indeed, before Hitler demanded to send his armies through Yugoslav territory to attack the British who, of course, had set themselves up at the time in Greece to help Greece. This was all terribly important to the Germans because the British were in Greece, and that's why Yugoslavia ran out of time in maintaining its neutrality, because Mussolini was losing the war to the Greeks and Hitler had to come to Mussolini's rescue in Greece, and that meant that countries like Yugoslavia simply had no time. They were going to be forced to abandon their neutrality one way or the other, either because they decided to side with the British and precipitate an immediate German-Italian attack, or because they decided to try to propitiate or make concessions to the Germans and would cause the British to wish -- to force them into the war, which is of course what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Very well. All the more so if you what you say is indeed true. If we look at pact again or the agreement, what was it that was so humiliating for the country, what was it that caused all the unrest and eventually the coup d'etat that you have referred to?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: What was so humiliating and so infuriating was that there was a pact at all. A very large portion of the especially Serb officer corps and various Serb nationalist sources and various Serb intellectuals and lots of people that the British were supporting not just in Serbia, but also, it has to be said, in Slovenia where there was tremendous opposition to the pact, these people were simply kind of having any kind of alliance with Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Your explanation is crystal clear. As an historian, do you know that prior to the signing of the pact, and you yourself said that you believed that the government did not do this willingly, had they previously tried to secure help from the allied powers, just in case they were made to sign the pact and just in case they were forced to go to war with Germany? And wasn't it, in fact, the case that despite their best intentions they said there was nothing that they could do for Yugoslavia, even if an attack was launched?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are right. Correct. The British offered lots of encouragement, but they couldn't offer anything else.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note, could Mr. Domazet be asked to speak into the microphone. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: If I'm not mistaken, there were some official statements made by the British leaders and statesmen encouraging the Serbs, invoking their history, and their former alliance, encouraging them to resist Germany and resist the pact itself. However, two days later, as you have just said, there was a coup d'etat. Their coup d'etat was preceded by rallies organised by people who didn't like the pact, to put it in quite simple terms. But much in history as we know it indicates that the British intelligence services and the British secret services had a significant role to play in this situation. They wooed those officers who were willing to resist Germany, who believed this to have constituted a humiliation for an act like that to be made and that this led to the coup that eventually occurred on the 27th of March. Would I be right in stating that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are indeed. Although of course historians still debate the exact degree to which the British were deeply involved in the coup, my own view, having researched these matters, is the British desperately wanted to produce a coup, were trying very hard to produce a coup, but didn't actually know the right people who could do the coup. And so they were very happy when the coup take place, but their contacts were rather peripheral. They were not deeply involved with Brigadier Boro Mirkovic, for examples, the man who actually carried it out. That was a surprise to them. But they did certainly help create an atmosphere in which army and air force officers moved to overthrow Prince Paul.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, could you move the microphone closer to you?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You mentioned Mirkovic. I have studied this, and there is much to indicate that he was one of the officers courted and eventually won over, so to speak, by the English, the British services, in order to achieve what all of the allies at the time were really interested in, not just the British. You don't seem to have that information, or perhaps for some reason this information has remained secret.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, actually, in this case the -- nothing remains secret anymore, but that doesn't mean that there aren't still puzzles. The British air attache, or really only the deputy air attache in Belgrade in 1941 claimed that he had been in close contact with Mirkovic and knew all about the plot. But the air attache was not himself part of the British intelligence services. It was called at that time section D, which was a part of the secret intelligence service. So there is still some ambiguity. Because the coup was seen not just by anti-axis Yugoslavs as a great heroic event, but it also was between by the British secret services as something that they could do amazingly effective things. Everyone wanted to believe that the British had been more deeply involved than was probably the case. I mean, they did help, there is no doubt about that, they helped as I said, encourage this to happen. But I think it would be a mistake nowadays to say that they pulled the strings. I think we now know, thanks to the researches of people like Jozo Tomasevic, that it was -- Mirkovic did it himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I entirely agree that this would never have been possible had the mood that prevailed among the top-level officers in the army at the time been such that it was possible for a foreign service to bring this sort of thing about. The pact was declared null and void, and as early as the 6th of April Yugoslavia was subjected to air strikes and it was also attacked on the ground with no declarations of war preceding these acts. Would that seem to be a fair assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly is. But the pact was declared null and void by Hitler, and not by the new Simovic government, because once Simovic put his government together, he appreciated the enormity of the danger that faced Yugoslavia, in the same way that Prince Paul and Cinkar Markovic and Cvetkovic had seen it and desperately tried to reassure Berlin or to use Mussolini to reassure Berlin that even the new revolutionary government would respect the pact. Because they realised that the country's military situation would be utterly and totally hopeless, as indeed it proved when the Luftwaffe bombed Belgrade on the 6th of April and German troops streamed in from Bulgaria which was where the war was lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I entirely agree. My question may have been a little imprecise. It is true that the new government tried to drag things out and to appease, as it were, the axis powers, Hitler specifically. It failed, however, and Yugoslavia was attacked on the 6th of April. You said this yourself, I wanted to ask the same thing about Bulgaria The Germans had some of their troops in Bulgaria at the time already, although as you have suggested, they were interested in a corridor through Yugoslavia as well, but it's true that they had troops on that side, at that end, as it were, and much as was the case previously, during World War I, Yugoslavia was yet again attacked from Bulgaria, as it were, from that side, that's where the attack eventually came from. Isn't that right, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Would you agree, sir, you've probably studied this too, what were the slogans, the most important slogans used in Belgrade and the other cities at the time, this is in reference to Serbia first and foremost, I'm not sure about other parts of Yugoslavia, but you may know something about that. The two rallying cries, if you like, were, "a war is better than a pact," "better a grave than being a slave." These were the two prevailing slogans at the time, the battle cries, if you like. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. They were.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yugoslavia won the war eventually. Even historians seem to believe that even Germany, and they were obviously entertaining secret plans to attack Russia, would not have attacked Yugoslavia at the time if Hitler had not been particularly enraged by what had occurred. It was on the 6th of April, much earlier than the -- [indiscernible] than Russia that Yugoslavia was attacked is that correct, sirs?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, and the two are completely linked. Hitler had to eliminate the trouble he had on his southeastern flank because of the coup in Yugoslavia and the presence of British forces in Greece. He had to get rid of that problem in Greece and Yugoslavia before he could safely attack Russian, which he had already planned to do the. And the fact that there were British forces based in Greece was the -- was a real threat to Hitler, because they could use their air power to attack the Romanian airfields -- the Romanian oil fields, and Romanian oil was absolutely central to the German war machine. So it would not have been safe for the Germans to attack the Soviet Union in June 1941, if they didn't eliminate the problem represented by an uncertain Yugoslavia and a defiant Greece beforehand.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Just to remind ourselves, I believe we can agree on this, there was an agreement at the time, a pact between the Axis powers and the Soviet Union that there would be no mutual attacks. This was an unofficial plan. Officially, what was there was an agreement to avoid any mutual attacks. There was some sort of a formal agreement between these countries right?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Indeed. It was the Molotov-Ribbentrop pact that made the Second World War possible, and the German invasion of Poland.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. The war itself lasted only a brief while. The Yugoslav army capitulated in no time at all. My question: Is it true that even then there had been ethnic divisions leading to a break-up that some of the territory was not even being properly defended, that the real fighting was conducted in some parts of Serbia, the Yugoslav army made headway into the Albanian territory, they had even entered territory, territory belonging to another country, but because of the odds they were facing they were soon forced to capitulate. Would that be a fair assessment?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: By and large, yes. The reason why the Yugoslav army sought to penetrate Albanian territory was to secure there, as Churchill was encouraging them to do, the supposedly vast stores of armourments that the Italians had. Since the British couldn't offer the Yugoslavs anything and the Americans could only offer money, in the short term, the question of armourments was crucial. But also of course there was the notion of repeating what had happened in 1915, with the government going into exile from some place like Albania or Corfu off the coast of Albania. So, yes. And you're also right to suggest that there was a massive disaffection in certain parts of Yugoslavia when the Germans arrived. This, however was not militarily significant because the battle had already been lost by the initial German incursion across the border from Bulgaria, which had destroyed any possibility of the Yugoslav army retreating any large numbers into Greece and joining with the British and the Greeks there. So the war was lost and, knowing that the war was lost, it happens to be the case that, you know, the Germans were rather welcomed when they paraded into Zagreb several days later. The war was lost even before it began, of course, in any sort of real historical terms. It was a contest of completely and utterly unequal forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: By all means. That is precisely what I think too. It wasn't an equal contest. But we have seen footage of the German army's entry, both into Zagreb and Belgrade, and I think those were two contrasting images and the contrast seemed pretty stark. Therefore, my question, is it true that the German army, the occupying army, was met with a great deal of enthusiasm in Zagreb according to the accounts of some historians, the only place they received a warmer welcome was, in fact, in Linz, Austria?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I don't know about the comparison with Linz but the German forces were received well in Zagreb. The reason being of course is that the -- Hitler it taken the calculated decision that the Croats would be rewarded and Serbs would be punished and the Croat's reward would be the creation of the Independent State of Croatia, and therefore winning Croatian support, making the Croats into an ally was something that Hitler was determined to do, because he was equally determined that, as an Austrian, and an Austrian who supposedly blamed Serbs for the break up of the Habsburg monarchy, had never forgiven them for 1914, that whether Yugoslavia would be destroyed as an idea utterly and totally. And so therefore the principal beneficiary of the Third Reich on the territory of the former Yugoslavia was meant to be the Croats, who were rewarded with this very large Croatian state, including all of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but, of course, as you will recall from my report this Croatian state supposedly independent Croatian state, was compromised at the outset by virtue of the fact that Hitler's Italian allies insisted on incorporating Dalmatia, which was really rather more dear to most Croats, something that was more important to them, than were bits and pieces of Central Bosnia. I don't think a lot of Croats were terribly excited by incorporating Foca, for example, Eastern Bosnia, Visegrad in the new Croatian state. So Hitler's attempt to appeal to the Croats was rather disabled at the very beginning by virtue of the territorial arrangements that he insisted upon, but even more of course by the fact that he had trusted the government of Croatia to an out and out gangster and criminal, Ante Pavlic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree that what happened marked the death of the Yugoslav idea, at least as far as the Slovenes and Croats were concerned, it spelt a defeat for Yugoslavia and the ideas promoted back in 1918, jointly promoted by the statesmen at that time?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is exactly what Hitler intended, that the Yugoslav idea should be destroyed for all time. But in that respect, as in so many others, Hitler proved utterly and totally wrong. The Yugoslav idea was reborn in the course of the resistance struggle led by the communists. And it was reborn in a new way whereby the Communists fought both for the recreation of Yugoslavia, but also for the recognition of the individual south Slav nations' proper place in that new Yugoslavia. At least that is, of course, the theory. What they were fighting for, of course, was total Communist power. But they made a very, very good use of the Yugoslav idea and caused the Yugoslav idea to have another 50-some years of life, and of course it's not impossible that it will come alive again, although utterly dead now.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Can we agree when you refer to the Communists at the time, that they raised their voice only after the attack on the Soviet Union. This was in June, I think.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: By and large, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: And another thing, would I be right in saying that after the capitulation of the Yugoslav army, the officers of that army and the men were taken to imprisonment, mostly in Germany, but only those who were of Serb nationality, not officers and soldiers from Croatia, Slovenia, and some other areas?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are correct, Mr. Domazet, it was Serb officers who in particular who were sent to prisoner of war camps, at least those Serb officers who hadn't managed to escape surrender or capture.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: You have already mentioned this, but let's remember that Serbia had the status of an occupied country, fully under German command. The Independent State of Croatia was established, which encompassed Bosnia and Herzegovina but not Dalmatia which was occupied by Italy, and the Independent State of Croatia stretched as far as Zemun in the east. Am I right?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Did this circumstance cause a migration of the population or what is called ethnic cleansing in territories where Serbs had lived, did they move towards Serbia, even though it was occupied from the territories of the Independent State of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: They did indeed. They did not only move, many were killed and others forcibly converted to Roman Catholicism. The ideology of the Ustasha state was that Croats had to become a convincing majority in this expanded Croatian state, and that could only happen if roughly one-third of the Serbs were got rid of by forcing them out, one-third were got rid of by murder, mass murder, and one-third were got rid of by forcibly conversions to Roman Catholicism that is that they would be made Croats, made into Croats, that the Bosnian -- excuse me, the Croatian Ustasha state could also only have a majority if it changed the national ideology of Bosnian Muslims. They had to be convinced that they were in fact Croats of Islamic faith, this was a huge effort which, of course, thankfully, the Ustasha regime was not capable of implementing in full, although, of course, the extent to which it did implement it was ghastly as it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you for your replies, Dr. Wheeler.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it is time for our break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Domazet. May the Chamber point out that we have gone for a session and a half now, and have reached roughly 1942. We would be very grateful if we could reach 1991 much more quickly. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.31 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Wheeler, you probably remember, we last discussed your explanations about what happened after the creation of the Independent State of Croatia, and its policies as far as Serbs were concerned, you defined it by referring to one-third, the second-third and the third-third. One-third were supposed to be murdered, another third were supposed to be expelled, and the third-third were supposed to be converted. Did that plan come to anything in the end, or was it for the most part implemented eventually?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It was implemented to a horrifying degree, but that doesn't mean that it was implemented in full, in part because the Germans, aghast and I should say the Germans and the Italians, aghast at the chaos which it proposed, the way in which it served to stimulate armed resistance, and thereby to remove any benefit to the Axis occupying regime from actually possessing this territory, the Germans and the Italians by and large started putting a stop to it in 1942. A stop to it in 1942, I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But based also on information which you discuss in your report, your findings seem to indicate that about 344.000 Serbs were killed in the Independent State of Croatia during the war. Would that seem to be correct, because that follows from your report, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I was -- I was citing the historical research in the 1980s of Bogoljub Kocovic. In the 1980s, as I indicated in the report, both a Croatian statistician and a Serbian statistician came up with roughly the same figures which I think are extremely well grounded and had the effect of course of contradicting what an awful lot of the post-Second World War mythology about absolute and relative losses amongst the various south Slav and non-south Slav citizens of the Yugoslav state had been. The figure of 340-some thousand Serbs who were killed or lost their lives in the Ustasha state, however, can't necessarily be put down to Ustasha policies. It would have been for a variety of reasons, and of course some of those deaths might have occurred -- I was going to say outside the bounds of the Croatian state, in the sense that that was territory not necessarily under Croatian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Indeed. At any rate though, these figures are impressive. They are large-scale figures. When discussing the estimated total of victims throughout Yugoslavia, you probably refer to that figure of about 700.000 [as interpreted], which would roughly amount to 10 per cent of the pre-war population of Yugoslavia. I suppose that was what you had in mind. A correction for the transcript. I said 1.700.000.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: The figure of 1.700.000 which was the conventional figure for the wartime death toll was a figure that the new Communist regime put together in 1946 in order to justify their reparations claims on the defeated Axis states. It was not an exercise in serious statistical or demographic or historic research. It was a guess based on a need to come up with a figure immediately. The subsequent serious research, which I cited in my report, pushed that figure down to just over one million persons. We are, of course, seeing ago similar phenomenon going on today in relation to the death toll in the wars of the 1990s. Vastly inflated figures were cited immediately after the 1991, 1995 wars, which for example said that the death toll in Bosnia and Herzegovina was something like 250.000 or at least 200.000. We now know because of serious research which has been done, that the death toll is probably more like 100.000. Now, these are still huge and scarifying figures but they put the previous guesses and estimates into some sort of perspective.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Indeed. You describe this in report too. That's a fact, but it's also a fact that you agree with the assessments that the Serbs who lost their lives in the Independent State of Croatia, that their numbers roughly amounted to this figure. As far as the total was concerned, the total of the Serbs who lost their lives according to Kocovic, which is also the figure you cite, 487.000. Most of the Serbs did come to grief in the territory of the Independent State of Croatia, that seems to follow from these facts which would roughly amount to almost two-thirds [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Indeed. Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: For the transcript, I said about three-fourths, not two-thirds. At any rate, it's easy to do one's own math, if you use the one and the other figure, 487.000, and 334.000. When we talk about the Serbs killed in the Independent State of Croatia, would I be right in stating this. If one of the ways to do this was to kill civilians and throw them into pits and we all know that there were lots of those in those areas, pits, grottos, and these traces remained in a way. Another method was to use camps such as those at Jasenovac, Gradiska, and others. Does your information seem to corroborate this, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. There was of course also in the early days even much more horrifically brutal killings of Serb villagers herded into churches and burned alive. The same sorts of things, of course, that happened in the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina in the 1990s, although not to Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We have just mentioned Jasenovac. It was the briefest possible reference. As you have indicated, this caused a lot of debate in post-war Yugoslavia in terms of how many people were killed there. I would not like to go further into this, but you did say yourself that there were attempts on the Croatian side to reduce this figure, they were talking about 40.000 people killed in Jasenovac. On the other hand, a figure that was ascertained was 400.000, I think you yourself referred to between 60.000 and 80.000 people killed in Jasenovac. Isn't that what your report states, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I believe so. I can't remember exactly. Certainly some estimates were way too low and other estimates were way too high. I think we could take it for granted that the number is between 60 and 100.000. We will, of course, never know completely. The trouble of course with these figures is that they achieve a life of their own. This is -- this is the case in regard to the Second World War and of course it is still the case in regard to the wars of the 1990s. Every year in the spring Republika Srpska in Bosnia-Herzegovina continues to have a commemoration on that part of the Jasenovac complex which nowadays lies in Republika Srpska, and on each and every one of these years despite historical research, the number that is cited is always 700.000 dead at Jasenovac. Now, serious historians do not believe that it's 700.000 for nearly 20 years but that doesn't mean that an awful lot of people continue to believe these hideously inflated figures.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You will probably agree though that 100.000 or between 60.000 and 100.000 is very high, an astonishingly high figure for a single camp during the war?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: In Southeastern Europe, yes, indeed it is, because camps whether we're talking about the former Yugoslavia or Greece, were not industrial death facilities such as prevailed in other parts of the Third Reich, for example in Poland or Bohemia.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I asked you about the expulsion or the exodus of Serbs from territory under the Independent State of Croatia, we agreed that this was, in fact, the case and this was part of the state's plan. However, what I want to ask you is this: Are you aware of the fact that there were mass expulsions of Slovenes from Slovenia done by Germans, that these Slovenes were driven to Serbia and that Serbia took in a large number of Slovenes during the war. Some of them later remained in Serbia, most however returned to their home country. Is this a phenomenon that you're familiar are?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It is indeed. Because that portion of Slovenia, or we could now call Slovenia which was incorporated in the Reich, the Germans had the same plans there for the Slovenes as the Ustasha regime had for most Croats in -- excuse me, Ustasha regime had for Serbs in the Independent State of Croatia. That is, they intended to denationalise them, they intended to get rid of as many as they could and the remainder would be Germanised. But of course the bulk of Slovenia was under Italian occupation, it wasn't actually incorporated into the Third Reich.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. We're talking about the area around Maribor, I'm referring to that particular part of Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Needless to say, you followed statistical indicators about the population in various areas of Yugoslavia. In particular, you used the 1991 census. In this document a parallel is drawn to several earlier census, the first being from 1948 and then all the way up to 1991, which I believe to have been the last census, population census in the former Yugoslavia. This is the situation established after the foundation of the second Yugoslavia or Tito's Yugoslavia for easier reference. Did that in itself change the demographic make-up in relation to what it used to be prior to World War II in areas where there were a lot of Serbs on account of the expulsion and murder of a great number of Serbs, did that contribute to reducing the Serbian population in those particular areas?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, it did, also of course what contributed was the post-war industrialisation and urbanisation of what I mentioned before. That had the effect also of reducing absolute number, if not the relative number, of Serbs in certain so-called, as you referred to them, passive regions. So yes. And there also was, of course, simply the fact that birth rates developed differently. For a long time after the Second World War, the Bosnian Muslim birth rate was much higher than the Croat or Serb birthrate in Bosnia-Herzegovina, so the Bosnian Muslim share of the population grew. But of course as prosperity became greater in the late 1970s, well then those birth rates pretty much equalled out in Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Muslims were no longer growing faster than Serbs or Croats. Of course, where the -- the one part of the country where the changing demography, the relative demography was most notable were in those parts of Yugoslavia which were inhabited by large numbers of Albanians whose natural increase far outstripped those of the Slavs among whom they lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I am not inclined to dwell on Albanian populated areas. This is a special situation including the prohibitional [as interpreted] then-government from returning to Kosovo. I would now like to shift to Vukovar, which is what we are really interested in. According to post-war statistics which is what you, too, have established, there were large numbers of Serbs living in the area, almost equal to the number of Croats living in the area. My question is: Do you know that up to World War II, the ethnic situation was more or less the same and that the Serbs may even have prevailed, had been the predominant group prior to World War II as opposed to post-World War II. Is this something that you're familiar with?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I have to admit that I am not.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Fine. Secondly, we discussed passive areas. Can we agree that the Vukovar area is among the richest areas, both in terms of the land and in terms of general infrastructure. It always belonged to the richest parts of Yugoslavia, including the town of Vukovar itself. This was not the same situation as that faced by the so-called passive areas, including economic migration. I do not think that that sort of phenomenon could possibly be applied to Vukovar?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I agree with you. Vukovar was a huge net importer or recipient of people after the Second World War. There were vast tracts of land that had been abandoned by the Germans who used to be a very significant national minority in that part of the world. These Germans left with the Wehrmacht or were expelled afterwards by Tito's regime, and there were therefore large numbers of people from other parts of Yugoslavia, Serbs and Croats, who came in to occupy this land. But there was also large migration from other parts of Yugoslavia because Vukovar, particularly Borovo Selo, became a booming industrial complex after the Second World War. You know, I can't remember the exact figure, but something like 30.000 people worked in the Borovo factory itself, the footwear and rubber goods factory. So the demographic composition of Vukovar certainly altered because of its -- because of the -- because of the departure of Germans and the availability of jobs as industrialisation took hold. But as I told you before, I'm not aware of the -- how over the decades the relative proportion of Serbs vis-a-vis Croats changed. I'm afraid I just don't have those figures in my head at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you don't seem to have those at your fingertips, we won't dwell on that. But the situation was similar, there were even more Serbs than in the period under discussion. However, when you talk about these things, it's true that the Germans were leaving these areas, not only this particular area, but especially Banat. Both Serbs and Croats were brought in from other more passive areas. Do you know that particularly in Eastern Slavonia Croats were brought in from western Herzegovina, which, unlike eastern Herzegovina, is populated by Croats. A lot of people were brought in, even later on a lot of people were brought into Eastern Slavonia. Do you know about that, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed and one of the things that one would always here in the Vukovar area when I was living there were complaints by the people who had been there a long time about these Iseljenici, these people, these Iseljenici, these new-comers, both old-time Croat and Serb settler -- inhabitants complained about the alien attitudes of these people that came from the mountains or from the, you know, snake-infested rock-strewn landscape of Western Herzegovina or Lika or wherever.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. I agree. That seems to have been a problem anywhere, where there was a large-scale migration. A lot of time went by though, the second Yugoslavia lasted for a longer time than the first. In the first case it was only 23 years. We have heard a lot of evidence, especially from Croats, natives of the Vukovar area, who told us about relations between Croats and Serbs all the way up until 1989 and 1990 being very good, very fair, very respectful. Is this a conclusion that your research has corroborated?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Indeed. Whether we're talking about Eastern Slavonia or Western Slavonia, relations amongst Serbs and Croats in both those parts of Croatia were traditionally extremely good.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Those were areas, as we agreed a while ago, that were economically more developed than some other parts of Yugoslavia. When you speak about Borovo, would I be right to say that the factory that you have referred to existed before the war? It was the well-known Bata factory, and after the war the existing factory just resumed work as usual, it was a well-known factory in European terms, the Bata factory?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, it was, but it grew hugely after the Second World War and became a real kumbanat [phoen] in its own right, instead of just making shoes for the Czech parent company.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. We're still talking about statistics, and the overview you gave us about the number of Serbs. You found that based on the census of 1991 the total population of Serbs on the territory of Croatia amounted to about 12 per cent. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That's, of course, what the 1991 census says.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. In the same report, however, there are other censuses, 1948, 1953 and 1961, and also 1971, where this percentage was between 14 and 15 per cent, and this was a constant throughout those years. Have you any explanation for this quite significant fall in the percentage of the Serb population in Croatia in 1991 as opposed to the percentage in the other years after the war?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, the easiest explanation for that is that since national identity is matter of choice, each and every one of us can decide that we are French or Russian or Serb or Croat, and no one can say otherwise. Especially, of course, amongst the south Slavs who were ethnically identical, all of them, in other words racially identical, I can only conclude that the -- aside from a long-term economically-induced changes in patterns of residence, which might reduce the number of Serbs in Croatia, the number of people who chose to call themselves Serbs in a census in 1991 could have reflected the rising tension at that time, especially, say, amongst Serbs who had long lived in big Croatian cities and found that it might be safer, more convenient, a good idea, especially, for example, if they were in mixed marriages, to claim to be something other than Serbs. The atmosphere was such, I mean this is why we saw of course the large reduction in the number of people who claimed to be Yugoslavs in 1991, throughout Yugoslavia. It was not a good year in which to be a Yugoslav. In some places it was not a good year to be a Serb, in other places it would have not been a good year to be a Croat.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. I fully agree with your explanation. I would like to go back to something I omitted to ask, so I will go back to that part. And it concerns your expert knowledge about when the new Yugoslavia was formed after 1945 in the then borders it had were the republican borders drawn up according to any special agreement? In other words, how are the so-called republican borders drawn up and did they have any practical significance up to the point when Yugoslavia dissolved?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: In most cases the borders of the new republics of the socialist federation were the historical borders. They were the historical borders of the previous provinces or regions or Kingdoms, whatever they might have been. There were, however, some exceptions and there were of course some big arguments about this. The area that the trial is concerned with was one of those areas where some violations of history were -- the historical borders were agreed, as you well know, I'm sure, the party set up a commission to investigate the area around -- the border of what was going to become the Autonomous Province of Vojvodina and the Croatian state. So there were some places where territorial changes were made, sometimes for economic reason, sometimes because of the way in which roads and railways went, more often because of national minorities or actually demography of the area. But by and large the borders were the historical borders of the pre-existing parts of the Yugoslav state. That was the case even where one might have thought it was rather strange, for example Bosnia-Herzegovina retained its tiny little stretch of Adriatic coastline at Neum which was a tribute to the former relationship between the Ottoman Empire and the republic of Dubrovnik, that was the border there, to separate Dubrovnik as an Ottoman satellite state from Venice to the north. On the other hand, Bosnia-Herzegovina also lost its tiny little exit to the Bay of Kotor and Herceg Novi. But by and large the borders were the historical border.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, you mentioned the example of Bosnia in your report. But referring to this historical circumstances, we agree that in the previous Yugoslavia there were no borders and the banovinas were arranged on a quite different basis and it was not possible then to conclude which parts of the territory belonged to Serbia, Croatia or Bosnia-Herzegovina, so can we agree that there were no such borders and that they were first established in Tito's Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: No. What Tito's Yugoslavia did is it reinstituted the historical borders that King Aleksandar had sought to get rid of. The -- the -- in its first ten years of existence, the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats, and Slovenes had maintained its recognition of the pre-existing historical borders. Aleksandar tried to get rid of them. Effectively, to put it crudely, Tito put them back.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Well, I can partly agree with you when talking about some borders of Serbia before the war, and even Bosnia-Herzegovina, which had been annexed by Austria-Hungary within certain borders, but what were the historical borders of Croatia and when they were they established, especially toward the east. For example, was Baranja ever a part of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're right. Baranja was never a part of Croatia. Baranja was simply a southern province of Hungary. But that doesn't mean that Croatia didn't have otherwise, in terms of the borders of Dalmatia, civil Croatia, and much of Slavonia, there were historical borders. But of course as you well know in much of central and eastern Europe, even historical borders are often argued about.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Croatia had, for many years, first been part of the Hungarian Kingdom and then part of the Austro-Hungarian monarchy, when did it have any historical borders as Croatia, rather than as a province of other countries?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: We could play games about this. Obviously there was once, in the 10th and 11th century an independent Kingdom of Croatia. It had borders. But the Croatia that we are nowadays thinking about, a modern Croatia, is really the borders that existed for Croatia inside the Habsburg monarchy. Now, of course Croatia's unique -- I shouldn't say unique. Croatia's unfortunate status of course was to have its -- what most Croats and certainly what most Croat legal scholars consider to be its historic borders violated by the way in which the Habsburg monarchy was set up. With Dalmatia belonging to Vienna, to put it crudely, and Istria belonging to various Italian provinces, and Slavonia and civil Croatia belonging of course to Hungary. But that didn't mean that there was not some recognition that there was a historic Croatian state, even if it was subdivided amongst the various parts of the Habsburg monarchy. One of the reasons why Croats were so completely frustrated in the 19th century and one of the reasons why their intellectuals gave birth to the Yugoslav idea was precisely this fragmentation of historical Croatia, as they regard it, the historical triune Kingdom of Dalmatia, Croatia, and Slavonia, by virtue of the vicissitudes of history and the gradual way in which the territory had been -- first of all, lost to the Hungarians and absorbed by the Habsburgs, and then of course conquered in large part by the Turks and then the way in which the tide was pushed back as the Habsburgs pushed the Turks back. So there is this sense of inhabiting a historic part -- historical kingdom in Europe that had been unfairly divided and subdivided and subdivided helped produce both the Yugoslav idea, but it also has to be said, the Croatian variant to fascism.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. You yourself spoke about the fact that the borders of the Croatian Banovina were misused for the purposes of acquiring territory, which objectively did not belong to Croatia. The banovina and the Independent State of Croatia extended as far as Belgrade almost, it extended as far as Zemun, it reached the Sava and Danube rivers. I just wanted us to try to agree that these borders were not evident and fixed and the population of course in those areas was mixed, it was both Croatian and Serbian. Looking at the statistics quoted in your report, we can see, and I hope you will agree, that there are even towns or villages, the population of which was almost 100 per cent Serb, such as Borovo and Trpinje for example. According to the last census, in Borovo there were 5.100-and-something Serbs compared to 604 Croats, or for example in Trpinje 1.953 Serbs as opposed to 73 Croats, and of course there were also Croatian places with similar percentages only a few kilometres away. So can we agree that this area was completely mixed and there were other ethnicities there, other nationalities such as Slovaks and Hungarians. But according to what we heard they lived quite well together until these events?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I will now move on to the last part of my part of the cross-examination. As I said, my colleagues will deal with other aspects, but they might touch on this because we feel that the situation in Vukovar in 1990 is extremely important, as were the events that occurred there. You mentioned the tensions, the fear that prevailed. Can you expand on this after all these various historical problems we have discussed, was the fear of the Serb population justified as a response to some moves made by the HDZ, Tudjman's party at the time, and I am referring in particular to some things that may not seem so important, such as changes police uniforms, introducing the chequer-board coat of arms which reminded many Serbs of Pavlic's insignia, and some other matters. Can you tell us if the Serb population was afraid? According to you, was that fear justified, whether it justified in being afraid that 1941 and the events of that year might be repeated again?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Fears on the part of Serbs in Tudjman's Croatia were justified. On the one hand they why justified because of the policies which Tudjman had promoted during his election campaign, the changes he made to the Croatian constitution after he won power. These fears were real. And Tudjman incited them. But it also has to be said that in large part these fears were incited by Belgrade. Ever since 1989 the Serbian-controlled media had been working to create fear on the part of Serbs who lived outside Serbia. So we had a wonderfully appropriate kind of synergy, in effect where, as the fears being incited from Belgrade were then further incited by the policies being adopted in Zagreb, and I -- the only thing I say in regard to Eastern Slavonia, is that it took greater effort in that traditionally peaceable part of the world for these fears to come to the surface. It had been much easier in Kninska Krajina and Lika and so forth to inflame Serb fears far earlier. It took a year longer to make Serbs in Eastern Slavonia, Baranja, and Srem as fearful as their brethren in these so-called passive regions had become by the spring of 1990, for example. So it took a year longer in Eastern Slavonia for the same fear to take hold and for then for the fear to be reciprocated on the part of Croats. There was simply a general rising sense of fear and tension amongst both Serbs and Croats. And if I had been writing this report now, as opposed to at the end of 1997, beginning of 1998, I might have paid more attention, because we now know much more, about for example the activities of Tomislav Mercep in the spring of 1991 in the Vukovar area. And we're about of course to learn more about the activities of Branimir Glavas who is about to be indicted. So we now have with the benefit of hindsight, given what this Court has produced in the intervening years, we can now see more exactly about how these fears in both communities were created intentionally by policy-makers or by in the case of Mercep, a freeboater, what I mean by that is an independent operator. So it's easier now to understand how there could have been a breakdown in trust and zajednicki or neighbourly relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: We have had occasion here to hear some explanations of certain incidents, explosions, fires and such like that took place. But less about killings which sowed additional fear. Do you have any information, any new information concerning the activities of Tomislav Mercep, he was active in Vukovar, and Glavas was active in Osijek, which was nearby. Can you give us any new informing about this now, about their activities and to what extent they could have imperilled the previous good relations between Serbs and Croats in that area?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I cannot give you any authoritative information because what I know is simply based on reading the press. I referred this morning to the heroic journalistic activity of the Feral Tribune, co-editor and correspondent in Osijek, Drago Hedl. Thanks to Drago I think we now know an awful lot more about the Croatian paramilitary or quasi-governmental forces. Similarly a lot of rather heroic journalists in Belgrade writing for Vranje over the years have investigated things as well. So I think it can certainly be said that we now have a broader understanding or the potential for having a broader understanding about the way in which the war came to Eastern Slavonia. But that doesn't alter the fact that there was a great Serbian project at the heart of the government in Belgrade which used such tactics for its own purposes. That's why I -- early this morning I said that I by and large stood by the thrust of my report, even though there were details that, if I were writing it today, I would write differently.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, I have heard what you said this morning. My colleague will go further into this area. To avoid repetition we have divided the topics among ourselves. I think you will have an opportunity to explain this further. But now, to conclude my part, you are certainly familiar with what the president of Croatia, Tudjman, was doing at the time to get Croatia internationally recognised. Can you confirm that one of the problems he had just before Vukovar was Gospic and the events that had taken place there in 1991. That is, the murders of Serbian civilians for which the Croatian army or paramilitary had been accused of. There wasn't a real Croatian army at the time. Do you remember what problems he had due to that with the international community?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes. He had the same problems that he had had from the very beginning of the Serb village and town rebellion, you know from the Balvan Revolution on, and that is that the Croats were seen by the international media and therefore foreign government as being very, very ham-fisted and brutal in some of the activities they took. And as a consequence something like Gospic renowned very much to the new Tudjman regime although it must be mentioned now that there have been trials of these people. That is, the Croatian government has since been able to come to terms with some of the crimes that were committed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes, if I understood you correctly, the international community was aware of this and this was one of the obstacles perhaps at the time for the recognition of Croatia. My next question, and my last question, is would you agree with me that what happened in Vukovar, especially the problem that arose because of the tragedy at Ovcara, had a decisive influence on the international recognition of Croatia and that it actually helped Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed the concluding point I made in my report. And that was that the combination of the brutality of the siege and fall of Vukovar, and the simultaneous omnipresence of pictures, the bombardment of Dubrovnik, had the effect internationally of making Franjo Tudjman and his regime look very good in comparison to the regime in Belgrade and that from the Croatian international -- from the point of view of the Croatian government's international position, the atrocities that attended the fall of Vukovar as well as the crimes against the world, architectural, historical, environment in Dubrovnik were a propaganda God-send, or a God-send in propaganda terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you. This also refers to the crime at Ovcara, which is the subject of our interest here, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: [No audible response] Thank you, Professor. Thank you for your answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have completed my part of the cross-examination, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, the reply to my last yes, indeed, has not entered the transcript. It's missing from the record. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, all.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, I am Mira Tapuskovic I am one of the Defence counsel appearing for Mr. Miroslav Radic. In 1998 you testified before this Tribunal in the Dokmanovic case, and the topic of your testimony was the same report we have before us today; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In your report, and during your testimony in the Dokmanovic case, you spoke about constitutional issues and the problems faced by Yugoslavia from 1974 until 1991; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will deal with these issues today as you touched on it in the Dokmanovic case, but we shall try to avoid repeating what was said in that case. We will only try to expand a little to encompass issues that are of interest to the Defence teams and could be of interest to Their Honours, especially as we have not had constitutional experts testifying in this case. Would you agree with me that from the time when Yugoslavia was established under this name it had a relatively turbulent constitutional history throughout its existence?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, it certainly did. As Mr. Domazet said earlier, in citing my views, Yugoslavia needed to make many, many attempts to find a satisfactory constitutional set-up for the multi-national state that it was. And, in fact, from 1921 onwards, there were six constitutions.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We won't go that far back, so we'll only deal with the constitutional history after World War II. First there was the 1946 constitution when the country was called the democratic federative Yugoslavia, is that correct? Please state your reply audibly so that it enters the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed of the first constitution, 1946 constitution is a Yugoslav copy of Stalin's 1936 Soviet constitution. The next constitution in 1953 represents the break with Stalin and the beginning of the real Yugoslav experiment in creating a new kind of socialism.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time the change was changed to Federal People's Republic of Yugoslavia and self-management was introduced?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It was the beginnings of the experiment of self-management, that didn't come properly until 1963 when the name of course was changed again to the Socijalisticka Federativna Republika Jugoslavija.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the experiment of introducing self-management on the territory of the former Yugoslavia remained just that, an experiment which did not yield any significant results, especially in the field of the economy?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: In retrospect, we can say that self-management was a delusion. At the time a great many of people found it exciting, potentially full of promise, and a wonderful way of somehow squaring the circle between Soviet-style socialism and western-style capitalism. It -- it in Kardelj's thinking, that's Edvard Kardelj. In his thinking it was a way of reuniting Marxism with Libertarianism. Again, in retrospect, a disaster economically. But it was a rather exciting disaster when people still believed in it. Excuse me, it was a rather exciting experiment when people still believed in it. And a lot of people did, and not just in Yugoslavia. It's very difficult now throughout the former Yugoslavia to cause people to recall how much they used to believe in the old system. Well, there were an awful lot of people in western Europe and the United States who also thought that self-management socialism was potentially a very great thing. It's easy to make fun of it now. In the 1960s and early 1970s, it looked pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was going to be kinder than you, I was going to call it just an experiment. You have described it in more pejorative terms. After 1963, when a new constitution was passed, and the country was renamed the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, until the next constitution of 1974, there was a period with much constitutional activity. There were about 40 amendments made to the constitution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The amendments of 1971 were especially significant. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Remind me what the amendments of 1971 were.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The amendments of 1971 gave rise to much outrage among professors at the university in Belgrade who spoke about the status of Serbia within the community and as a response to the protest of the professors at the faculty of law in Belgrade, they were stricken off the list of professors, Vojislav Kostunica was one of them, the present day prime minister. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What about those constitutional amendments, do they coincide in terms of chronology with the emergence of the so-called maspok in Croatia in 1971.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, they coincide with the emergence of the so-called maspok as well as so-called wanton liberalism. In Marko Nikezic, in the Serbian communist party, and in the Slovene Communist party at the same time. These were years of tremendous ferment, excitement, liberalisation, argument, in very, very many spheres. It's not for nothing either that they were highly, highly creative period in terms of literature and cinema in Yugoslavia. This was an exciting period, and lots of things were being argued about all the time. It was a period in which you could argue about things out in public all the time. And people didn't exactly know where the limits were. What would happen if you said, you know, something too extreme. It was -- it was a time of great ferment and eventually of course would give rise to what you're going to come to next, which is the amalgamation of all these amendments that you talked about in the 1974 constitution which was meant to somehow, for all time, sum up this long period of social, political argument, cultural effusion and it has to be said also, the complete rebirth of the national question in Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you can agree with me on this, there was a period of rest and peace along the ethnic lines, but then when the maspok movement emerged in Croatia in 1971 there was a reawakening so to speak, a re-opening of the national question throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Although it -- it actually hadn't started in Croatia, it really started with Serb alarm already in 1968 over what was happening in Kosovo. Or even before that, you could say that it started in Slovenia, with great arguments over road-building. From -- from 1963 onwards more and more of the republican governments started playing the nationalist card. They started trying to enlist popular support when they wanted to fight their battles in Belgrade over who got what in terms of national expenditure, how investment decisions were made, and so playing to the national constituency, playing to the gallery became more and more of a habit of Yugoslav politicians of all national persuasions. But certainly the maspok was the first instance where a republican communist party itself gave way tremendously to an intellectual and popular sentiment, in this case that Croatia had been unfairly treated for many years.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me, won't you, that Croatia's position at the time was that all of Yugoslavia's financial means were flowing down the Danube on to Belgrade, as it were, and after quite a long time this was a renewed attempt to have the state itself decentralised in a way, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Would you agree with me that if we look at all these names, let alone all the later name changes, I mean the names of the country itself, it became Federal Republic of Yugoslavia as of 1992 and now we have the Union of Serbia and Montenegro. Would you agree with me that each of these different names preserved or in some way reflected the socio-political form or structure of the country itself, the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federative National Republic of Yugoslavia, and the Socialist Republic of Yugoslavia, all these names in some way reflected the make-up of the country itself, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, up until, of course, now. And there will be another change after Sunday.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would not like to venture into that territory now. Let us please go back to the 1974 constitution. That is what the Defence teams here are really interested in. We believe that this constitution provided a framework for what happened later in the former Yugoslavia. The shape of things that were to come as it were. In the Dokmanovic trial you gave evidence, sir, and you said that you had read the 1974 constitution. Do you remember saying that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I certainly remember saying it, but I -- it's not one of my favourite pieces of bedside reading and I have not gone back to read it since. I think the only time I ever did read it was when it was brand new and exciting and we all thought that it was the way ahead. So sometime after 1974.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you are an expert in Slavic studies, if I may call you that and you follow closely whatever is going on in the former Yugoslavia I'm sure that you will be perfectly able to provide all the answers that we want. You will agree with me that the 1974 constitution was the longest, the most comprehensive or extensive constitution in the world at the time, probably, and it was marked by lousy legalese, to say the least. It was also described as a constitution that introduced a number of new legal institutes and concepts hitherto unknown in the legal practice of any existing countries or systems. Would you agree with me, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I agree with you wholeheartedly. Not only did it introduce amazing, crazy terminology, but in the post-socialist Yugoslav republics, we are still having to cope with it. Concepts like social property. Created a legal mess we still live with.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this constitution, which was passed after a series of amendments, its pre-history, so to speak, was quite stormy, in essence reflected a growing discontent among the peoples and ethnic groups and in the republics of the former Yugoslavia. Furthermore, it reflected their desire to have their relations arranged in a more decentralised way than had up to that point been the case. Would you agree with that assessment, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact, however, that the constitution had a certain objective, and was meant to lead to decentralisation and as a consequence a greater level of democracy throughout Yugoslavia's society, what it did was bring about a much higher degree of separatism throughout the former Yugoslavia. Would you agree with my assessment that at the time the republics in a way became autarkic economic systems that existed side by side within the country.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That was certainly the trend at the time but the full extent of that, of course, was only going to become apparent after Tito's death. And it wasn't the 1974 constitution itself, the 1974 constitution gave a legal basis for what had already, from the mid-1960s, been a developing trend of the republics regarding themselves in ever more autarkic terms and battles with one another over investment decisions and effectively a share of the federal budget. So the 1974 constitution didn't stop an already apparent trend, and, in fact, it gave it ever greater weight once Tito was no longer on the scene to settle these battles, to make the decisions. What the 1974 constitution was also supposed to do was to recognise the reality, the reality that had developed since the early 1960s of the republics becoming evermore independent-minded, evermore selfish, too, it has to be said. But it was supposed to reconcile this reality with the counter-veiling force of a supposedly forever united League of Communists. So the republics would be more a more autonomous, but Tito hoped, after defeating the maspok and getting rid of Nikezic and purging the Slovene party, Tito hoped that the party would always be united and, of course, that the JNA would always be united. So it would be a balance of forces. That, in any case, was Edvard Kardelj's idea.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that essentially the constitution merely reflected the reality that had been in existence for some time that carried over as it were from the previous system. Would you agree with me that all the new constitution did was provide a legal framework for something that was already there, objectively speaking. The republics were drifting further and further apart and becoming, to all practical intents, self-governing or autarkic republican economies?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I agree with you essentially, but what the 1974 constitution also did and I'm surprised you haven't mentioned this already, is it gave effectively gave both Vojvodina and Kosovo republican status. Not formally, but factually. Which of course part of Serbian grievances against the 1974 constitution.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That is quite correct, I was about to ask you some questions about that at a later stage. But my idea of this cross-examination was go through the economic background first, since I believe this to have been the source of many other phenomena, and this is normally the case in any country or any state. Not just the former Yugoslavia. I will now pursue a number of questions about the economic situation that was created, a situation that created conditions for economic development in what was then Yugoslavia. We seem to have agreed on the fact that the republican economies became autarkic or self-satisfied, if you like. Can we then agree on this: There was a duplication, perhaps a triplication and their industrial and production capacities. The use that these were put to were miserably negligent, the production was negligent. As a final consequence, this led to a sharp rise in poor development of the republican economies which ultimately contributed to impoverishing the country as a whole?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes. And that fact of course was obscured for a good many years by the results of the first oil crisis which meant that money was washing around the international system and every bank in the world was falling over each other, falling over its other -- every bank was falling over other banks to throw money at the -- at Yugoslavia. In other words, loans. The inefficiencies of the system, the duplication of the competition you talked about, the fact that going back -- there was a -- a strange combination of the way in which the socialist mentality that progress is only mentioned in -- is only -- is only -- excuse me, that progress can only be measured in terms of belching smokestacks, there was a unification of that socialist idea with increasing republican patriotism or republican self-interest which meant that every republic felt it had to have its own steel mill, for example. And this was made possible by virtue of the fact that there was lots and lots of money slashing around in the international system which international bankers were very keen to loan to Yugoslavia, creating of course the basis for the financial crisis in the 1980s. In the 1980s, I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Let's not go too far in that direction, and go on talking about economics. Let's go back to the constitution. Do you agree with me that the 1974 constitution regulated that the entire judiciary, the entire legislative power in the country should be devolved to the republics and that only vital legislation, vital for the whole country, should be kept at the state level, the army, the banks system, diplomacy, that sort of thing?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: By and large, yes. The federation legislature, the federation parliament, of course, still had effectively the power to enact what one might call framework legislation, to set the standards that the republics were supposed to obey. But by and large what the 1974 constitution did in practical terms if not in theoretical legal terms was to change the federation of Yugoslavia into a Confederation. There is to be no doubt about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I will now move on to a question that you broached a while ago, the question regarding the status of the autonomous provinces within Serbia itself. When did Serbia for the first time in its modern history come to have, as it were, these autonomous provinces? In 1946 in the aftermath of World War II, the autonomous provinces did not exist?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Their emergence was gradual. In the immediate aftermath of the Second World War, Vojvodina was an autonomous -- I can't -- was it "pokrajina"? I can't remember the term, but immediately after the war Kosovo had a lesser status, it was an autonomous something, and Vojvodina was a higher status. Later on in the 1960s, both Vojvodina and Kosovo acquired the status of autonomous region. Autonomous province, pokrajina. I think Vojvodina was a pokrajina from the start in 1946. It took longer for that same dignity - I can't remember now the exact year - to be awarded to Kosovo-Metohija which originally had a lesser standing than Vojvodina, if only because, of course, there was a rebellion going there, going on there after the Second World War.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We've already concluded that the names were changed quite often, the name of the country, the name of its various institution, ministries, secretariats, it wouldn't be a wise idea to foist too many of these upon the Trial Chamber. Vojvodina was a province, but it was no autonomous province, and that's why I asked my question about when these eventually emerged. Can you either confirm for us, sir, that Serbia only, in the former Yugoslavia, had such administrative units as these autonomous provinces, the autonomous province of Vojvodina and the autonomous province of Kosovo and Metohija. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... only Serbia was further subdivided along these lines. Although of course there had been plenty of ideas that a similar thing should be done to Croatia. During the war itself and immediately afterward there was talk of an autonomous Serbian province in Croatia. And, of course, the final map of the republics was something that was uncertain of until after the war. The fact that there would be republics, if the country would have a republican -- would --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just to have this on the record, I asked you about Serbia being the only republic within Yugoslavia that had autonomous provinces. You -- you said that you agreed. Can you just repeat that for me for the sake of the record, please.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Only Serbia had autonomous provinces within its frontiers.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
