utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now please try to explain this phenomenon. You said this yourself a while ago before I actually asked my question. The status of these autonomous provinces that were part of Serbia, and this is something that enemies of the constitution later characterised in the following way: In essence the autonomous provinces, as you yourself stated in the Dokmanovic trial, had nearly all the attributes of a republic. Which means that to all practical intents and purposes, what we had in Yugoslavia were eight separate republics. I'll try to illustrate this by using the example of constitutional amendments. This is probably the best illustration and will be easily comprehended by everyone here, how these amendments were applied in Serbia at the time. You do agree with me that all the republican and provincial constitutions had to be in keeping with the federal constitution of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, right?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Under the federal constitution amendments could only be introduced having previously obtained consent from the republican assemblies, in exceptional circumstances also that of the province -- provincial assemblies, the assemblies of the autonomous provinces. Do you remember that provision, sir?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I'm reading the transcript here, because I lost track of the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I will repeat my question for you, that's no problem. From my present angle it's very difficult to look at the screen and I should keep pressing away at this button here, to have it on my screen. Not practical, I'm sure you would agree. You say that you have not looked at this constitution for a great many years. Something about the 1974 constitution, the federal constitution, do you remember that it envisages amendments to the SFRY constitution only with the previous consent of the republics and [Realtime transcript read in error "in"] autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that the Serbian constitution contains provisions that describe the conditions required for any amendments to the constitution, the constitution can only be changed if changes apply to the whole territory of the republic in question, including the autonomous provinces, and amendments can only be made having previously obtained the consent of the assemblies of the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I can't say that I remember this, but I am sure you are absolutely right. I don't remember it from my reading, I've never read the Serbian constitution, but I'm sure you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it's 2.00 -- 3.00, rather. I have just been warned by my colleagues this might be a good time for us to have our afternoon break and then I can resume with my questions after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mrs. Tapuskovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to say that on page 88 of the transcript, line 16, when republics and autonomous provinces are mentioned, it should say not "in," but "and." Republics and autonomous provinces. Not "in."

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Wheeler, let's go back to where we left off before this short break. If I tell you that according to the republican constitution of the then Socialist Republic of Serbia for its constitution to be amended the consent first had to be gained of the assemblies of the autonomous provinces, would you accept this as correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Of course I would. And that's of course why, in 1999 Milosevic had to get the assemblies of Kosovo and Vojvodina to effectively abolish themselves. To accept, in other words, the unification of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will come back to 1999 -- or 1989.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now, let's talk about the provincial constitutions. According to the provincial constitution of Vojvodina, and that of Kosovo and Metohija, in order for the constitution to be changed there had to be the consent of two-thirds of the deputies in the assembly. Does this mean, Mr. Wheeler, that if the provincial assemblies decided on constitutional amendments the republican assembly did not even have to be informed, let alone ask for its consent, and if the republican assembly wanted to change the constitution, the provincial assemblies could use their veto power and block the constitutional amendments?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. As a historian, can you now tell me who could find this kind of constitutional situation congenial, who or what forces could find these kind of relations in the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia to suit their interests?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Are you referring exclusively to the anomalies of the constitutional situation in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, let's start from Serbia. I will reformulate my question. This kind of constitutional set-up, could it have suited Serbia's interests?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is a complicated question. The reason being is that sometimes states or in this case a republic of a federal state, find it useful or necessary to limit their own powers in order to meet the needs of various minorities of one sort or another. In other words, they self-limit their own sovereignty or the portion of sovereignty that they dispose of. The European Union would, of course, be a very good example of this same phenomenon whereby effectively small minorities in the form of small states can say no, and that can limit the ability of a huge majority of, say, big states to do what they want. So in complicated constitutional set-ups, sometimes a small minority can enjoy a hugely disproportionate amount of effective or legal constitutional power. And sometimes those big states or those big complicated constitutional arrangements find it necessary for their own health and potential longevity to limit their powers in that way by making sure that small parts of the state or small parts of the multi-state system have such extraordinary rights.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But regardless of whether incorporating such provisions in the highest law of a country is democratic or non-democratic, in any case it leads to paralysis of the constitutional system. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I would. It is an inherently inefficient way of running a government, in any state system. However, of course, as I said, sometimes it's thought to be a price that has to be paid. Just next door to the south of this country we have another complicated state in the form of Belgium, which pays a high price in terms of the need to constantly renegotiate the basis on which its people's co-exist. Today, of course, under the Dayton constitution in Bosnia-Herzegovina we have a similarly complicated and thereby restrictive and often hugely inefficient system of constitutional order. Inefficient constitutional order.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I agree with you. Would you agree with the following: Such phenomena in normal stable constitutional systems, where a constitution is amended once every dozen years or once in a century, but in a country that has gone through so many constitutional changes, and where one of the mottos of further development was that development continues, could such a constitutional provision in that situation have been an obstacle to further progress? Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: A -- complicated constitutional settlements are very often obstacles to progress, but as I said before, they are sometimes the price you pay for maintaining a complicated and especially multi-national state community. Another good example, of course, would be Switzerland which is changing its constitution all the time through popular referenda. Again, different kinds of state communities find different solutions, some of which are not from the outsider's point of view, efficient, but they can on the other hand be considered to be necessary in order it maintain the essential consensus among the people of a -- of a state or in a multi-state system, among the various individual components of that multi-state system they are necessary to maintain the consensus that keeps the system going. And so, yes, Yugoslavia, the federal Yugoslavia paid a very high price, and Serbia as a devolved unit of that federation, which had devolved provinces, also of course pay the price in terms of efficiency.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: In any case, none of the other republics within the former Yugoslavia had that problem. Serbia alone had that problem, and it was the most populous republic?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You are completely correct in formal terms. Although Bosnia-Herzegovina as a multi-national -- you know, completely multi-national republic in the structure of the former Yugoslavia, of course, also had to engage in informal negotiation over changes. In other words, the national complexity of any country, whether it's -- whether it is accommodated by formal arrangements or informal arrangements still has to be accommodated.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But you will agree that regardless of its multi-ethnicity, Bosnia and Herzegovina was sovereign on all of its territory, whereas Serbia was sovereign only over a narrow part of Serbia, leaving out the autonomous provinces?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, let's move on. This situation lasted for 15 years in Serbia until March 1989 when constitutional amendments were introduced. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At that time this step taken by Serbia where you say that it abolished the autonomous provinces, was commented upon, both internationally and by public opinion within the former Yugoslavia, and you termed it an attack on the 1974 constitution when you testified in the Dokmanovic case. It was seen as Serbian hegemony and restoration of a sort of centralism?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: It was seen in retrospect as potentially having that effect. As it happened, the other republics were, in 1989, perfectly happy to allow for Serbia to re-unify itself and not formally, but in effect abolish the autonomy of the autonomous provinces. But afterwards, as I said in both my testimony in the Dokmanovic case and in my report, the League of Communists of both Slovenia and Croatia and later Bosnia and Macedonia, had cause to regret that they had given way, because they began to fear that what had happened to Kosovo and Metohija on the one hand and Vojvodina on the other could happen one day to them, especially after the change of government in Titograd, in Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: If Serbia enacted its constitutional amendments in 1989, and established sovereignty on the entire territory of Serbia, and in practically the same year Slovenia enacted its own amendments to the Slovenian constitution and then issued -- or rather, Croatia issued a declaration with almost the same legal consequences, would you agree with me that this was a trend among the Yugoslav peoples to establish full control over the territory of their own states as far removed as possible from the central government?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes indeed. Both Slovenia and then later Croatia followed the Serbian example and, in fact, in some ways even want farther by declaring the superiority of their own constitutions to that of the federal constitution. But Serbia had led the way.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Someone had to be the first, and the other republics went down the same road almost at the same time. You will, however, agree with me that Serbia established its authority only on its own territory without nulling the federal constitutional provisions, whereas Slovenia enacted legislation to the effect that the federal constitution and laws could apply on the territory of Slovenia only if they did not run counter to the Slovenian constitution and laws. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is correct. Although something like a year and a half had elapsed between the reunification of Serbia in early 1989 and the passage of constitutional amendments in Slovenia, which gave the Slovene constitution primacy over the federal constitution. And, of course, in the meantime the republican government in Titograd had been overthrown by people in favour of Milosevic and that meant that effectively Milosevic had four votes in the federation Presidency and the four votes in the federation Presidency, the effect of that had a profound effect in both Zagreb and Ljubljana, as far as alerting them to this supposed new Serbian threat, this hegemonism that you referred to before.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I mentioned [indiscernible] hegemony because the introduction of amendments to the Serbian constitution was characterised as such. Can you tell me whether you recall how the international public and public opinion within the -- within the then Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia described the Slovenian declaration and the practical annulling of the federal constitution? What was said about this move by the Slovenian authorities? Serbia was termed a hegemonistic country.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, we -- we need to make a distinction between how people abroad regarded this and how it was regarded at home in Yugoslavia. There was a considerable degree of informed opinion abroad as there was amongst those people in Yugoslavia who still believed in Yugoslavia to regard what was going on as a -- and what Milosevic in particular was promoting, a degree of recentralisation. There was a tendency both abroad and in Yugoslavia initially to regard this as a necessary thing. As you were implying before in your questions about the complexity of the constitutional arrangements. It was widely believed as the economy deteriorated after Tito's death, and as the -- and as his successors proved completely and utterly incapable of coping with the rampant inflation and economic decline, it was believed that the constitutional structure was unnecessarily, in fact dysfunctionally standing in the way of any sort of improvement. And this -- this inclination to regard a certain measure of recentralisation in Yugoslavia as a good thing was very wide-spread, especially in western capitals. It was also something that quite a lot of people believed in, in Yugoslavia itself, who threw up their hands often and said, This system is crazy. Won't work. We have to have something new. And there was then a period when there was more wide-spread approval for the -- for the changes which Milosevic was believed to stand for when we think back to the anti-bureaucratic revolution and all that, there was a great deal of indulgence shown to that idea, both abroad and in educated circles throughout Yugoslavia. By the time the Slovenes on the other hand declared the superiority of their constitution over that of the federation, the mood had rather changed, I think, abroad, as well as certainly in the Slovene and -- and Croatian communist parties. Because, remember, they walked out of the last federal party congress in January 1990, and it's -- that's kind of the turning point, it seems to me, where people both inside Yugoslavia, who believed that there was some recentralisation necessary and people outside of Yugoslavia who certainly thought that recentralisation would be a good idea to a certain extent, I think that's the point at which they began to have doubts about whether or not Milosevic was a good thing and whether or not he was the potential agent for positive change that had seemed in some places -- at least an idea you could argue in favour of, say in 1988, 1989. But after January 1990, I think that were there was not any particular inclination to condemn the Slovenes for doing what they did, although an awful lot of the international media shared the view coming out of Belgrade that the Slovenes were being typically and totally self-interested, selfish, and you know, looking after themselves.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come back to that later. Let's go back now to the 1974 constitution, both the federal and the republican constitution. I assume you recall that in the preamble the 1974 constitution gave the peoples of Yugoslavia, not the republics, but the peoples guarantees for their right to self-determination, including the right to secession. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: That is indeed the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was it a rule that those nations which were of south Slav origin were elevated to the status of nations, whereas those who were not of south Slav origin were not constituent nations under the constitution, which was valid. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I -- I agree fully. The distinction between "narod" and "narodnosti" was a very important one in Yugoslav constitutional practice and it had also profound effects.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Can we agree then that the right to secession, that is to self-determination, including secession, was also guaranteed in the republican constitutions of all the republics within the socialist federative republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you perhaps explain, in scholarly terms, why when Croatia and Slovenia seceded, they used the term "dissociation", rather than using the constitutional terms that is it self-determination, including the right to secession?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: In practical terms the reason why dissociation was used was because even as they declared their independence they weren't necessarily certain, that is the Tudjman or the Kucan regimes, they weren't necessarily certain that it was going to work, that they would be successful. In a sense they were still making a bid for a -- continuing negotiations on a new form of Yugoslavia as an alliance of sovereign republics. To put it in colloquial English terms, they were hedging their bets, they were seeking not to go so far that they would not be able to come back, if somehow they would get a better offer for a new kind of Yugoslavia. And it's for this reason that I put such emphasis in my report that the fact that really marks the final break-up of Yugoslavia is when the fighting starts, when the army moves into Slovenia. Because even those declarations of independence which had been much heralded in the case of Slovenia, rather rushed through in the case of Croatia, were not seen as necessarily final acts, because the -- the endless meetings of the republican leaders had been going on. People found it very difficult to believe that there was life after Yugoslavia, in other words, they -- there was profound public scepticism in the early months of 1991 about whether or not this state which had endured for 74 years, would finally break apart. There was a feeling that maybe some last-minute solution would be found. And I think that's why they used the term "dissociation." However, it could be that there was a constitutional legal reason that I haven't thought of.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see whether we can unearth that reason. You agreed with me that the constitution of the SFRY envisaged the right to self-determination, including secession and that it guaranteed that right to the nations of Yugoslavia, that this was not a right reserved for the republics.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, but that's also complicated, as so many things were in Yugoslavia. By virtue of the fact that the republics had come to embody the sovereign rights of the peoples who lived in them. So that meant that Serbia was the sovereign republic of the Serbs, Croatia of the Croats, Slovenia of the Slovenes, Macedonia of the Macedonians, Montenegro of the Montenegrins. It was only in Bosnia-Herzegovina that there was no constituent people. No people of state. Although, of course, in the case of Croatia Serbs and other south Slavs were also constituent peoples before Tudjman changed the constitution. But that didn't alter the fact that in practical terms the Croats were the people of state.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that when referenda were held in both Slovenia and Croatia a referendum was held within a republic, and that the right to vote in a referendum belonged to the electorate of that particular republic. Would you agree with me there?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: At the referenda, both in Croatia and in Slovenia, the population or the electorate voted, and they could be members of different nations or nationalities, but it was not the entire nation that was voting as envisaged by the constitution of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: No, but the republics had become -- the republics had become each of them, other than Bosnia-Herzegovina, associated with one particular nation. So obviously in the referendum regarding Croatian independence, Croats in Serbia or Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina did not vote in that referendum. Similarly -- but on the other hand, everybody in Croatia, whatever their national identity might be, was entitled to vote. The political problem, of course, arose because of Serbs, having had their own referendum prior to the official Croatian referendum in the spring of 1991, did not vote. And of course then the same thing would happen in the case of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The fact that there were -- that nations, individual south Slav nations were spread across many republics was a complicating factor to this notion that only nations had the right to national self-determination. But another complicating factor, of course, was that the right to national self-determination was a notional right in any case, because communist legal theory held that that right had been exercised for all time in 1943. Or whenever each -- whenever any one of the avnoj [phoen] bodies, zavnobik [phoen] and its Croatian and Serbian, whatever, whenever those bodies had met in 1943 in the case of Croatia and Bosnia, in 1944 in the case of Macedonia, I can't remember about Montenegro, and, in fact, not until 1946, I think, in the case of Serbia. When that -- that had been the one -- once and for all time exercise of national self-determination. So we shouldn't get too hung up or pay too much attention to the language in the 1974 constitution because it was in some ways simply paying tribute to the ancestry of an act of self-determination, which, as far as Communists were concerned, had taken place in the past and would never take place again in future.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I accept your explanation. Provided that someone from the remaining republics wishes to exercise their rights, then they would try to find a possibility to have the constitution interpreted in a more liberal way. But when Serbia tried to interpret in a more liberal way its own sovereignty in its territory, this was, in fact, disallowed. I read to you the preamble to the SFRY constitution where it states that the nations of the SFRY enjoy the right of self-determination and secession. What I meant is that Croats or Slovenes residing anywhere in the SFRY territory had the right to vote. However, they didn't have the right to vote. Although, in Croatia, as you rightly pointed out, the Serbs did not take part in the referendum. Do you not believe that this application of the constitutional provision envisages the right to self-determination and secession, or rather the terming of any actions taken as disassociation constituted a violation of the then-existing constitution of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I'm sure that a very sound constitutional legal argument can be made to the effect that it was a violation of the constitution. But an apologist for what the Croats and the Slovenes did, would equally point out, an apologist would say we'll just following in the tracks of out, an apologist would say we'll just following in the tracks of what Milosevic has already done. But these constitutional arguments are in some senses irrelevant because of course the daily development of political life goes its own way regardless of constitutional niceties and in any case the intervention of foreign states made it necessary to hold these referenda in any case. You know of course I'm referring to Badinter Commission and so forth. So real life sometimes gets in the way of constitutional law. And real life always wins.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What you have just stated is the position declared by the European Union at the time. They claimed that the real situation, the situation on the ground, was something that had to be accepted, regardless of the fact that in the formal sense of the word, at least, not all the conditions had been met for international recognition. The standards required at the time by international practice, control of territory, effective authorities, and contact or interaction with other countries and states. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I -- I agree with you, yes. They were making it up as they went along.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'll try to finish my cross-examination of the witness by the end of today.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you now a couple of questions about certain legal documents that were created in the republics of the SFRY causing commotion, both domestically and internationally. You referred to some of these in the Dokmanovic trial. What I would like to discuss with you is the issue of the memorandum in Serbia back in 1986, sometimes erroneously referred to as the memorandum of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences. You will agree with plea that the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences never acknowledged this document as their own, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I will indeed agree with you, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You will agree with me that this is -- this is a document which saw the light of day in one way or another, it was stolen at one point and subsequently published. You will agree, won't you?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I said that a certain number of members of the Serbian Academy of Arts and Sciences, if indeed they had authored this document, are not an accurate reflection of Serbia's intelligentsia at the time, as it were?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: The strand of thought represented by the draft memorandum that was stolen and published turned out to be electrifying for many Serbs wherever they were in Yugoslavia. It turned out to be terrifying for many non-Serbs wherever they were in Yugoslavia, and, of course, it was also a matter of considerable shame and regret and disagreement on the part of many Serbs as well. So, yes, the SANU -- the draft SANU -- what's referred to as the SANU memorandum split opinion. A considerable number of people approved of it and found it extremely exciting that the truth was finally will be told about Serbia's diminished position. Other Serb, other Serbs and including intellectuals were alarmed by it. The party, of course, officially, was alarmed by it and denounced it. But it's one of these documents which in retrospect, despite being unofficial, had a profound effect on changing the nature of the political climate and the nature of political debate throughout Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: That's all right. Now, I'd like to share with all the other players in this trial what the document was about. Would you agree with me that the author or a group of authors used this document, usually referred to as a memorandum, to present a number of problems and difficulties faced by Serbia at the time or in the immediate past, as well as to predict certain problems that Serbia was likely to be facing in future.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me if I put it to you that this document, despite everything, in no way suggested that the break-up of Yugoslavia was Serbia's only solution?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: No, of course it not -- of course it didn't. The most profound effect it had, however, was in alarming non-Serbs about the way in which a significant portion of Serbian intellectual thought was moving and the extent to which these Serbs were profoundly dissatisfied with the sort of Yugoslavia that had been formally ratified in the 1974 constitution, if not well before. The -- the basic thesis which the memorandum attacked, that a weak Serbia was necessary for a strong Yugoslavia, was revealed, of course, by the reactions, both among Serbs and by non-Serbs, to unfortunately be correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you remember these events from personal experience or based on your research, your research in the history of the Balkans. I do hope that you remember even before the memorandum a Slovene magazine called Nova Revija, a Ljubljana-based magazine, published a platform for an independent Slovenia calling for Slovenia's secession from Yugoslavia in no uncertain terms.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, indeed, I certainly remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that this document published by this magazine, the independent Slovenia platform, was not branded as an act of outrageous nationalism or being the Bible of Slovene nationalism, whereas on the other hand the memorandum was certainly branded as a mark of Serbian nationalism and as something showing the way for Serbia's future?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I disagree with you there. The -- the platform in Nova Revija was certainly characterised both in Yugoslavia and abroad as an exercise in Slovene nationalism. The difference between the reactions, mostly critical at the time -- in retrospect, of course, Slovenes in particular would say that it was a heroic start to an ultimately victorious effort to create an independent Slovene republic, the difference of course is that the Slovenes whether decided to stay in or leave Yugoslavia were not in a position to destroy Yugoslavia, that was a privilege reserved to the Serbs as the largest and most wide-spread of the south Slav peoples. So when the Serbs, whose nationalism is always a particularly sensitive matter for non-Serbs, start evidencing the kinds of grievances and discontents and anger that were given evidence of in the so-called SANU memorandum, it's a more serious matter. It's a more serious matter for the future of Yugoslavia. Because the Serbs are the people at the heart of the state, the idea, the people who have the idea that they've built the state, who can most easily and expeditiously destroy the state.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I see, and I'm talking about page 105, line 7, that you stated to get today -- restated something that you wrote in your report already, that the Serbian people had the privilege of destroying the common state, of destroying Yugoslavia. This is page 16 -- or rather page 14 of your report. That is the B/C/S reference. I think the English reference is page 16. You, I believe, use these very words?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Since this is something you've mentioned already, this is the second last sentence of that paragraph. You say, "That privilege was reserved for the Serbs." Both in your report and in your testimony you have confirmed for us that the Serbian people were the most committed of all to a Yugoslav orientation, that they were the most numerous among those advocating the Yugoslav idea, if you like, because they very keenly felt the need to preserve Yugoslavia. Can you then explain, sir, if Serbs had so much at stake in preserving Yugoslavia, and if all these people declaring themselves as Yugoslavs, having so much at stake in preserving Yugoslavia -- or, rather, could we draw a parallel there? You seem to suggest both in your report and on the record today that the privilege was reserved for the Serbs to destroy Yugoslavia. Can you please elaborate on that a little? For me, this appears to be a contradiction in terms. If on the one hand the Serbs were the ethnic group present in all the other territories of the SFRY of the former Yugoslavia, the most spread out, if you like. In essence Serbs were the most numerous group, the most numerous single group, how then can one possibly arrive at this conclusion, the privilege to destroy Yugoslavia was reserved for the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I should apologise for quoting myself, but it's a rather good turn of phrase, and by using it I was trying to indicate not something that's a contradiction in terms as you suggested, but rather a paradox. A paradox whereby something that by and large most Serbs for most of the time, and certainly most foreign friends of Yugoslavia had regarded as one of the principal arguments in favour of maintaining a Yugoslav state, and that is that it was a state that allowed all Serbs to live together in one country, that it was paradoxical that those same people who got the most in some ways out of living in Yugoslavia should have been the -- should have been the people who turned on it and initiated a process which led to its violent dissolution. It's a paradox. And a tragic, tragic one.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Let us say that we accept this explanation. We don't have that much time left. I would like to deal with something that we have called disassociation or secession in relation to two Yugoslav republics in particular, first Slovenia and then Croatia. This triggered a conflict throughout the former Yugoslavia. You're familiar with the fact that between January 1991 and throughout the summer of 1991, there were all kinds of paramilitary units operating throughout the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes. There certainly were ever more paramilitary units. However, I would take you up on one of the point you made. And that is there was some low-level conflict going on well before Slovenia and Croatia declared their independence. In other words, from the summer of 1990 in Croatia itself there was a localised Serb revolt frequently referred to as the Balvan revolution, the log revolution. So it -- you know before the -- Milosevic's -- excuse me. Tudjman's election in itself in April and May 1990 was enough to start a process that indeed, as you suggested, became unstoppable after the 25th of June, 1991. But it took it nearly a year for it to happen.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to go back to my previous question and we'll come to this eventually as well. I'm sure you know that there were attempts by the federal bodies while the Presidency was still functioning properly and I'm talking about July, 1991, proposals were made to bestow certain powers on the federal bodies to have all the paramilitary units disarmed within a two-week period. This decision was to be signed by the then federal president. This happened to be President Mesic at the time. Are you familiar with the fact that he actually refused to sign that decision, the decision to disarm paramilitary units throughout Yugoslav territory?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I am aware that that is what has been written. Yes, I am aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you explain, sir, how it was that paramilitary units in Croatia got their weapons?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Are we talking about Croatian paramilitary units or Serbian --

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: The Croatian ones.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Well, they would have achieved -- they would have acquired weapons via a variety of means. Some weapons from the former teritorijalna odbrana, from the Territorial Defence units fell into their arms, although no where near as much as had been the case in Slovenia. Other arms were being bought on a massive scale insofar as they could be smuggled across the borders, especially from Hungary and of course it was also the case throughout Yugoslavia that people who lived in the countryside tended to have arms. There were an awful lot of arms around, hunting rifles in any case. But prodigious efforts were made after the summer of 1990 in Croatia to set up armed militias and then private entrepreneurs, we mentioned Mercep before, were also setting up their own militias. There was on the other hand, no particular problem in acquiring arms for Serbian paramilitary or Territorial Defence unit organisations because, of course, they had easy access to the Territorial Defence armouries and of course were also armed by the Yugoslav People's Army. The Croats had to struggle very hard and -- to get armourments.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: I deliberately asked you about the Croatian paramilitary units, because I think you will probably agree with me that up to August, 1991, Croatia did not have its own armed forces with the exception of the police, who also somehow had been successful in obtaining weapons. But there were no official armed forces, to put it that way?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: You're right. In the absence of an army, Tudjman had sought very hard to form what one might call sort of Carabinieri-style of police forces, in other words he would try to use certain units of the police -- special police units which had a military style to them and of course the police didn't have any shortage of arms. It's just they didn't have the kind of arms that might be necessary to do serious fighting. They obviously had kind of weaponry that policemen have. And that's why the smuggling operation from Hungary, the various efforts to buy weapons in other countries was so important.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: While answering the questions put to you by my colleague, Mr. Domazet, my learned friend, you talked about the fear that arose. I'm tying to keep my questions short I only have a couple of minutes to complete my cross-examination. The fear felt by the different ethnic groups because of the developments around them that were felt to be out of control. Would you agree with me that in a situation in which the Serbian people in Croatia are -- were seeing memories of Jasenovac being conjured up, they are seeing Croats arm themselves all around them on a massive scale. As you have just pointed out, they are seeing the status of their own people being reduced from that of a constituent group to that of a national minority, they were seeing their own Cyrillic alphabet being abolished and this was always a hallmark of the Serbs as a nation. Would you agree with me that there is a collective memory of the Serbian people dating back to the aftermath of World War II, this collective memory is now slowly being transformed into collective fear. Fear. Fear of history repeating itself?

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: I can agree with you almost completely on that. With the one reservation that a tremendous amount of effort was made by the Belgrade media and latterly by the Zagreb media to create just that sort of fear. That fear was there to be awakened, but it was stimulated artificially. Radio-Television Belgrade broadcast, it seemed, pictures from Jasenovac virtually every day in those months. It was a fear which was stoked, but truly there was an awful lot of material there from the past which justified such fear, as well as, of course, the way in which developments were proceeding at the time. As far as the Cyrillic alphabet is concerned, if I might mention parenthetically, one of the amusing things for me during the time of Republika Srpska Krajina was to visit officials in Knin and Okucani and discover what difficulty they were having using the Cyrillic alphabet on their Cyrillic typewriters, having never before thought that that was necessary to do to be a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: My last question for you, sir. In June 1991 Slovenia and Croatia declared independence. Their international recognition was delayed for a variety of reasons. It wasn't before the 15th of January that these two states were recognised by the European Union and it wasn't before June 1992 that they became members of the UN. Would you agree with me that regardless of the warnings issued by the Secretary General of the UN not to rush the international recognition of Slovenia and Croatia, Germany decided to grant recognition to both Slovenia and Croatia as early as December.

utterances.speaker: MARK CRAWFORD WHEELER
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. The Germans were the most enthusiastic, or along with the Austrians, the most enthusiastic of those people who thought in Europe at the time that early recognition of Croatia would - Slovenia, of course, was already out of the picture - early recognition of Croatia would somehow help to stop the war. Stop the war in Croatia, but stop the war also from spreading to Bosnia-Herzegovina, that Belgrade would take the recognition as a profoundly important development and be frightened off. I mean, the Germans were wrong, but nonetheless the -- that was their -- that was their rationale. And the normal way of negotiating inside the European Community, as it still was about to become union, was this if any one country wanted something badly enough, if something was crucial for its own domestic politics, then by and large you could usually get it. And that's why the Germans were able to convince the other European powers to go along with them although, of course, the Germans announced their recognition a month before the other European Union [sic] countries did it.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I have a go at one last question, and this time I mean it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me, sir, that by granting international recognition to Slovenia and Croatia that this constituted a violation of the 1975 Helsinki Convention guaranteeing the non-viability in Europe, and that this was, in fact, done to legalise the situation on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: This witness is a historian. He is here to testify as to the facts, as to the constitution, basically the existence of a constitution and what was in it, as to the actions or the -- the circumstances which arose as a result of a constitution or a law, or a law that was enacted. This, however, goes to the issue of being a constitutional scholar. This is a legal question, and it is outside his level of expertise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We think, Mr. Weiner, your one objection for the day must succeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I thank you very much. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Ms. Tapuskovic. We will now adjourn and look forward to tomorrow at 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of May, 2006, at 9.00 a.m.
